# Picking Your Child's Height and IQ - Hacking Darwin

- Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=hyqA7x1KzhU
- Published (UTC): 2022-07-19T01:07:03+00:00
- Source: consolidated from timestamped transcript; NOT independently fact-checked

### G001 [00:00:00–00:01:31]

[00:00:00] Julius presents a hypothetical fertility-clinic visit in 2035. Ten years earlier, “you” used IVF and embryo screening to avoid a serious, life-altering single-gene mutation; your healthy 10-year-old daughter has strengthened your confidence in screening. At school, you have also seen children with genetic abnormalities you believe could have been avoided if their parents had conceived in a lab rather than through intercourse.

[00:00:39] Back at the clinic, you tell the doctor you want to repeat the experience. The doctor says that is what everybody says and offers a cappuccino, leading you to think assisted reproduction has become a more competitive customer-service business as its popularity grew. The doctor says you were ahead of your time in having ten eggs fertilized; you have slept easier knowing the other nine embryos remained frozen and have decided you want another child. The doctor suggests thawing six and extracting five cells from each for preimplantation genetic testing.

### G002 [00:01:33–00:03:06]

[00:01:33] In the hypothetical, you agree. The doctor explains that a decade earlier screening covered single-gene mutation disorders and simple traits such as hair and eye color; knowledge has since expanded to multigene patterns associated with complex disorders, including some appearing later in life. Because patterns vary between people and the whole genome remains poorly understood, this analysis is only directionally predictive, not the binary on/off outcome described for single-gene disorders.

[00:02:18] The doctor illustrates a percentage prediction: an embryo might have a 70% chance of producing a child who develops disease X before age Y. This means elevated likelihood, not certainty, and excludes post-birth environmental factors. Predictions cover serious, painful genetically influenced diseases, including familial Alzheimer’s, heart disease and some cancers. Selection cannot avoid all disease but could improve a future child’s odds of delaying or avoiding it. You remark that much has changed.

### G003 [00:03:09–00:04:36]

[00:03:09] The hypothetical doctor says the law requires asking whether you want predictive information, which you may refuse or request by signing a tablet. You sign, reasoning that you must choose an embryo anyway and might as well choose one with the greatest chance of a healthy life.

[00:03:33] The doctor must also separately ask whether you want probabilities for non-disease traits if embryos are implanted and carried to term. You stiffen and ask what traits; the doctor cites gene patterns suggesting greater chances of a longer, healthier life. Relieved, you call that a no-brainer and consistent with your purpose. The doctor says some people grow nervous as screening moves further from disease prevention, but many diseases correlate with age, so fighting disease also requires defending children against aging.

[00:04:20] You note that others accuse doctors of playing God. The doctor smiles wistfully and acknowledges that some think assisted reproduction goes too far, offering choices nature or their deity did not intend humans to have.

### G004 [00:04:38–00:06:04]

[00:04:38] The hypothetical doctor says it is important to learn what each parent is comfortable with and help achieve it. You say you would have had more qualms ten years ago, but now see failing to select embryos most likely to have a long, healthy life as taking something from the future child: not adding healthy years, but preventing their loss.

[00:05:00] As you reach to sign, the doctor stops you: longevity is only one screen; height can also be predicted very accurately. You recall reading that taller people tend to have higher incomes and self-esteem; the doctor says most studies suggest this. You wonder whether a couple of inches justify choosing another embryo, then reason that all are your potential natural children, and, other things being equal, choosing a taller child is simply not choosing a shorter one. Already selecting for so much else, you decide “why not.”

[00:05:41] The stylus feels heavier as the doctor stops you again and introduces IQ screening. Despite having seen news coverage, you feel uncomfortable choosing a future child’s potential IQ and ask how accurate the test is, partly to stall.

### G005 [00:06:06–00:07:34]

[00:06:06] The hypothetical doctor says IQ predictions are probabilistic and improving; upbringing and education matter, but IQ is mostly genetic, particularly with age. Asked whether a higher-IQ child would be happier, she says no one knows: IQ remains controversial and is called culturally biased, though society itself may also be culturally biased. She nevertheless claims IQ correlates with many important life outcomes.

[00:06:39] You wonder whether you want to choose your child’s brain function and whether an unoptimized child would love or hate you for it. The doctor says repeated international studies associate higher IQ with longer average life. As an example, she describes Scotland testing all its 11-year-olds on one day in the 1930s; six decades later, researchers connected scores with life experiences and found higher-scoring children lived longer on average even after controlling for social class and other factors. She says scores of further studies found the same.

[00:07:23] Reluctant to reduce your future child’s identity to survey results, you ask how this can be known when IQ is not one thing. The doctor agrees IQ is complicated and often rejected, adding that some say a high IQ does not even make someone smart.

### G006 [00:07:36–00:09:08]

[00:07:36] In the hypothetical, you ask whether higher IQ makes someone a better artist, more loyal friend or more loving parent. The doctor calls these the right questions and says there is no evidence for any of those outcomes, but claims substantial statistical research strongly correlates high IQ with success at school, career, wealth creation and social ability.

[00:07:59] You begin to relent: IQ does not measure everything and a person is more than a score, but rejecting it could make your child suffer if you are wrong. Choosing another embryo would not guarantee a greater genetic predisposition to artistry or compassion; those qualities might also correlate positively with IQ, though you do not know. Your gut now suggests something is wrong not with selecting a relatively higher-IQ embryo, but with *not* selecting it. You recognize this as politically incorrect but feel the moment requires brutal honesty.

[00:08:47] You squeeze the stylus and look up. Gravely, the doctor says there is more: recent research on personality styles. A lump forms in your throat as you ask what mystery will remain in a human being; the doctor begins to invoke people you know.

### G007 [00:09:10–00:10:50]

[00:09:10] In the hypothetical scenario Julius reads, the doctor discusses personality differences, including extroversion, openness, neuroticism, sadism and cruelty. She says personality styles have many foundations, but genetics is probably the largest. The prospective parent, thinking of their sister, asks whether they can identify the next Mother Teresa or Jeffrey Dahmer among the frozen embryos.

[00:09:39] Unsure whether the parent is joking, the doctor cautiously explains that genetic patterns underlying personality styles are beginning to be understood, and that people selecting embryos are legally entitled to this information if they first sign a waiver. She agrees personality cannot be reduced to genetics, but says the parent can receive statistical probabilities and select whichever of their six embryos is comparatively most likely to have the desired personality style.

[00:10:34] The parent objects that this feels like ordering a child from Starbucks: light milk, an extra espresso shot and three pumps of mocha. The doctor says she is not trying to persuade them, only explaining their options; the decision is theirs.

### G008 [00:10:52–00:12:19]

[00:10:52] In the scenario, the parent recalls surprising their parents with mathematical ability when neither could balance a checkbook, overcoming shyness to sing in a school talent show, and life’s unfolding mysteries. They wonder whether selecting traits from a menu would change those experiences or their parents’ pride—whether the performance would have seemed foreordained if they had been genetically optimized for extroversion.

[00:11:19] The parent counters that all the embryos are their natural children, and one will be born into a world where other parents make the same choices. If they will spend decades helping their child flourish, why not choose the embryo with the best chance? Their arm quivers and they squeeze the stylus, wondering whether to sign.

[00:11:51] Julius identifies the reading as a hypothetical from *Hacking Darwin* by Jamie Metzl, but says such a choice may not be far off. He claims DNA sequencing has fallen from millions of dollars per person to a few hundred and might cost as little as $80 in a few years.

### G009 [00:12:21–00:13:09]

[00:12:21] Julius says that, with people’s permission to compare their DNA with their actual physical and mental traits, sequencing more people could reveal much more than single-gene mutation diseases or traits; the transcript’s example sounds like “iron hair color.” He predicts that multi-gene patterns will become clearer as the available data grows, making the scenario a matter of time.

[00:12:45] He asks viewers whether they would choose to receive the information and invites comments on the traits they would prioritize, such as height or IQ. He asks them to subscribe, enable notifications and perhaps share the video with a friend to see whether they agree or disagree, then wishes viewers a nice day.

# How To ACTUALLY Increase Your Lifespan - Hacking Darwin

- Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=icGRanS0brA
- Published (UTC): 2022-07-27T02:04:58+00:00
- Source: consolidated from timestamped transcript; NOT independently fact-checked

### G001 [00:00:00–00:01:32]

- [00:00:00] Julius recounts that “mustai” died too, and King Gilgamesh wept. A tavern keeper warned that human life is short and only gods live forever, but Gilgamesh sought immortality anyway; Julius says he failed because a snake “finessed” him. That does not mean everyone must fail too—or perhaps they will.
- [00:00:22] He introduces a strictly scientific discussion of increasing lifespan, inspired by Jamie Metzl’s *Hacking Darwin*. He asks why muscle fibers begin to disappear in one’s twenties, bodily functions peak in the late twenties, death risk doubles every eight years from age 30, and cells lose mutation-repair capacity around 40.
- [00:00:47] He says historical average human lifespan was about 18: people risked death in childbirth or from early infections, and later from accidents or predators. He gives averages of 47 in the United States in 1900, when it was among the most advanced countries; 72 worldwide today, 79 in the United States, 85 in Japan, and around 50 in many of the poorest African countries. Understanding the complex nature of aging, he says, is the first step toward considering future potential lifespan.

### G002 [00:01:33–00:03:06]

- [00:01:33] Julius lists scientists’ differing conceptions of aging: changes increasing an organism’s likelihood of death; progressive functional decline; increased inflammation or oxidative damage; or declining ability to activate stem cells needed for cell repair.
- [00:01:50] He calls aging the leading cause of human death because major killers are aging-related: heart disease, cancer and chronic lower respiratory disease account for over half of US deaths. He argues that curing one disease leaves others; eliminating cancer in the US would add only about three to four years of life expectancy. Extending overall lifespan therefore requires focusing less on individual diseases and more on slowing aging itself.
- [00:02:27] He says scores of studies reportedly show calorie restriction extends life in yeast, flies, worms, mice, rats and other organisms, although long-lived mammals and humans take much longer to study. In macaque studies begun in the 1980s—macaques share 93% of human DNA, he says—calorie-restricted monkeys lived three years longer on average and remained healthier than unrestricted monkeys in the same conditions.

### G003 [00:03:08–00:04:37]

- [00:03:08] Julius says at least four monkeys in one study surpassed prior longevity records for captive macaques, results he calls beyond promising. He attributes the effect to a caloric deficit lowering metabolism and the “rate of living,” thus reducing cellular work and wear and tear.
- [00:03:38] He cautions against a perpetual caloric deficit: metabolism would keep adjusting until calorie intake was insufficient for survival, so restriction can become unhealthy. He suggests occasional deficits or short water fasts may benefit long-term health by lowering metabolism, which could then be maintained at a new maintenance calorie level.
- [00:04:06] He criticizes society’s promotion of body positivity as irresponsible to the species because, in his view, it encourages disregard for health. Saying “cancel me if you wish,” he calls for acknowledging health implications instead of virtue signaling or companies boosting their ESG score. He reiterates that he is not recommending long-term deficits, but claims long-term surpluses harm health and lifespan by raising metabolism and cellular wear.

### G004 [00:04:39–00:06:18]

- [00:04:39] Julius cites a study following over 650,000 people for an average of ten years and analyzing nearly 100,000 death records. Compared with frequent couch-sitting, he says, 75 minutes of moderate exercise weekly corresponded to almost two extra years of life expectancy; 2.5–5 hours to 3.5 years; and an hour daily, or 450 minutes weekly, to about 4.5 years. He considers a few extra years from exercise and reduced metabolism worthwhile but not amazing.
- [00:05:20] Asking what “super agers” over 100, such as “Gene Kalman,” are doing, he says their longevity is more about winning the genetic lottery. He introduces Nir Barzilai, director of the Institute for Aging Research at Albert Einstein College of Medicine, as a leading aging expert. Julius says Barzilai and colleagues found centenarians did not develop Parkinson’s, Alzheimer’s and cardiovascular disease at the higher rates expected.
- [00:05:53] He says the team identified a gene transcribed as “apipoq,” common in most people but absent in these super agers, whose absence appears to protect against arterial inflammation. Other researchers have identified tens of genes whose various expressions appear to protect against brain disorders and elevated cholesterol, further protect against Alzheimer’s, and generally increase lifespan; he says more are being found rapidly.

### G005 [00:06:20–00:08:00]

- [00:06:20] Julius predicts that more DNA sequencing will identify more longevity-related genes. Parents using IVF embryo selection might choose embryos with or without particular genes, and advances in genetic engineering might permit intentional modifications. He refers viewers to his recent genetic-engineering video, noting that such approaches would not help someone already alive, only a future child in the distant future.
- [00:06:53] He says declining cellular NAD+—nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide—is one reason DNA repair weakens with age. NAD amplifies the activity of seven sirtuin genes, improving DNA repair; more cellular NAD means better repair. He reports that Harvard scientist David Sinclair and colleagues engineered mice to express high levels of something transcribed as “sarcoid,” or used NMN to increase NAD, finding better organ function, endurance, disease resistance, blood flow and longevity than in same-aged mice.
- [00:07:36] He says human trials are only beginning, yet the market for unregulated NMN and NR supplements is already booming. He introduces metformin as another drug shifting cellular activity from growth to repair: doctors have prescribed it since the 1950s, and the US FDA approved it in 1994 to help diabetics control blood sugar.

### G006 [00:08:02–00:09:54]

- [00:08:02] Julius says 80 million metformin prescriptions are filled annually in the US. He cites a 2005 study finding reduced cancer risk in diabetics taking it, a 2014 study finding they outlived both untreated diabetics and non-diabetic controls, and a mouse study finding treated males lived 6% longer on average.
- [00:08:26] He says scientists concluded metformin affects entire organisms rather than only individual diseases, making people more like genetically fortunate centenarians such as “Gene Kalman.” His explanation is that insulin signals cells to grow; too much, like overeating at a dessert bar, leads cells to overinvest in growth rather than repair. He says moderating insulin uptake through diet, exercise, calorie restriction or metformin shifts cells back to repair, reducing oxidative stress like long-lived quahog clams and improving disease resistance like naked mole rats.
- [00:09:05] He calls NAD boosters and metformin potential early drugs targeting aging, but not the last. He says rapamycin has extended life in all animals tested in studies worldwide; its ability to slow targeted cell proliferation and growth made it an immunosuppressant for preventing transplant rejection. Doctors then noticed people taking it seemed healthier than similarly situated animals and people. After a gap in the transcript, he says shifting cellular energy from growth to repair explains why a drug with that effect could improve longevity.

### G007 [00:09:57–00:11:25]

- [00:09:57] Julius says the previously discussed drug is not suggested because it suppresses the immune system, leaving people vulnerable to other diseases. In a transplant situation, he calls its use making the best of a bad situation: someone who needs a transplant to live is willing to sacrifice other things.
- [00:10:12] He says young, healthy cells divide regularly to replace themselves, but some stop dividing with age. Instead of dying and being flushed out, these “zombie-like” senescent cells secrete molecules that increase inflammation and tissue damage. They also suppress cancer-cell and tumor growth, however, so he proposes pruning rather than eliminating them.
- [00:10:37] He says mice in which scientists genetically engineered and activated a transgenic suicide gene lived 25% longer, regrew lost hair, and had stronger muscles and better-functioning organs. He describes a race to develop and test “senolytic” drugs to prune senescent cells, treat specific aging-related diseases, and potentially extend health span and lifespan.
- [00:11:02] Julius calls blood-swapping studies extremely interesting and says that, despite its clichéd portrayal in TV and movies, substantial scientific evidence supports it. He is considering a dedicated video. Concluding, he says that for someone without gifted genetics like Jeanne Calment’s, the best current option is to shift cell activity from growth to repair.

### G008 [00:11:27–00:12:18]

- [00:11:27] Julius completes his claim that shifting cell activity toward repair can increase lifespan. He says he cannot advocate taking any of the drugs mentioned, but suggests regular exercise and not overeating a surplus; he does not suggest fasting or even temporary deficits.
- [00:11:45] He says he is not a doctor and does not know; he read a very interesting book and wanted to share one of its chapters. He offers a description link to *Hacking Darwin*, asks viewers to subscribe and share with a buddy, and signs off: “Stay curious, stay skeptical, have a great day.” A standalone “you” is heard at the end.

# The ONLY Way To Distinguish The PAST From FUTURE - Explained

Repeated button presses make no visible difference, and you wonder whether the button is broken or you are moving forward or backward. Fearing you will be stuck forever unless you find the precise present, you remember physics class and examine how a group of molecules’ speeds increase or decrease after each click: “Eureka,” you can make it out alive. [00:01:26] Julius proposes that time is not merely unnecessary for describing physics but should be forgotten altogether: it has no role at the fundamental level. This raises the problem of how to preserve and describe notions central to human experience.

[00:01:54] He says up and down never enter Newton’s equations, yet mean something near a planet or other sufficiently massive, gravitational body: down is toward that mass and up is the contrary direction. Similarly, hot and cold do not exist at the microscopic level, but heat emerges when many microscopic constituents are described by averages; a hot body has an increased average speed of its individual constituents.

[00:02:35] Thus “hot” and “down” are comprehensible in particular circumstances—averages of many molecules and a sufficiently large mass, respectively. Julius says something similar must apply to time: although it has no fundamental role in physics, it matters notably in human life.

### G003 [00:02:57–00:04:30]

[00:02:57] Continuing the comparison with up/down and hot/cold, Julius asks what the passage of time means. He suggests that time’s origin, like heat’s, may derive from averages of microscopic variables, and claims that every phenomenon in which we notice time passing also involves temperature.

[00:03:20] He says time moves forward, not backward, and some phenomena are irreversible. Mechanical phenomena—described in the transcript as those that “don’t involve e”—are reversible: a pendulum looks realistic on film even when reversed. A ball hitting the ground, by contrast, looks unrealistic in reverse when it rises spontaneously; he says its energy heats the ground, and producing heat at that moment makes the process irreversible. He quotes Carlo Rovelli’s *Reality Is Not What It Seems*: “It is always heat and only heat that distinguishes the past from the future.”

[00:04:10] Julius applies this to ordinary phenomena: a burning candle becomes smoke that cannot be turned back into a candle, producing heat; a boiling cup of tea cools rather than heating up, diffusing heat into the air; and humans produce heat as they live and age.

### G004 [00:04:32–00:06:01]

[00:04:32] Continuing his examples, Julius says car tires wear over time while friction produces heat—noticeable if touched after a drive. The sun ages, produces heat, and will eventually exhaust its combustible hydrogen and die. [00:05:05] He reiterates that any phenomenon certifying time’s passage does so through heat production. He attributes to Rovelli the statement that there is no preferred direction of time without heat, while heat names averages over many variables. Thermal time reverses the usual question: instead of asking how time produces heat dissipation, it asks how heat produces time.

[00:05:30] Julius credits Ludwig Boltzmann with understanding heat as arising from observed averages. He says Boltzmann died by suicide, potentially because few people then took his idea seriously, and that his entropy equation is on his tombstone. Julius explains thermal time as likewise deriving from our interaction only with averages of many combined variables; with a complete description of a system described through averages, a variable can function like time.

### G005 [00:06:04–00:07:33]

[00:06:04] Julius completes the preceding thought: heat dissipates along this variable, which is the time experienced in daily life. He reiterates that time is not fundamental but appears to be because the world is immense and we are small systems interacting with macroscopic objects. Unlike the traveler in the imagined suit, we see balls, mountains, family members’ faces, and other things that make our perception of the world beautiful, not single elementary particles.

[00:06:38] He says a world without time is hard for humans to imagine: we live and dwell in time, are nourished by it, and are effects of temporality produced by averages of microscopic variables. Understanding the world sometimes requires going against intuition; otherwise it would be simple. He quotes Rovelli’s conclusion: “Time is an effect of our overlooking the physical micro states of things. Time is information we don’t have. Time is our ignorance.”

[00:00:00] Julius addresses dark energy as cruel: its accelerated expansion will make what is now visible within our Hubble radius disappear into darkness. He calls this merely the beginning of the end.

[00:00:35] Music introduces his multipart series on heat death, which he calls one of the most likely, arguably *the* most likely, endings of the universe. He promises to explain how it might give birth to a new universe, perhaps identical to ours. Earlier episodes introduced the concepts and explained accelerating expansion and the disappearance of distant galaxies; he calls today’s subject the darkest.

[00:01:23] Each dying super-galaxy will eventually be alone, without incoming gas to fuel new stars. Existing stars will burn out, exploding as supernovae or, more often, becoming slow-burning relics whose outer layers gradually cool over billions or trillions of years. Black holes will grow for a time: some will engulf galaxies’ worth of dead stellar remnants, while others will stall for lack of nearby matter.

### G002 [00:01:53–00:03:29]

[00:01:53] Julius says that after stars fade, ultimate decay begins, citing Katie Mack, author of *The End of Everything*: even black holes evaporate. Although most initially believed them eternal, Stephen Hawking calculated in the 1970s that quantum effects at their horizons make them glow. The glow draws energy and mass from the black hole; evaporation accelerates until it explodes and disappears at the end of its extremely long life. Even the massive black holes at galaxies’ centers will fade.

[00:02:36] Julius says planetary and stellar matter will also decay if left long enough because most matter particles are unstable; a neutron, for example, decays into a proton, electron and antineutrino. He gives an estimate of over 10³³ years and says even hydrogen atoms, the universe’s most abundant, will decay after that period. He again blames dark energy for the fade to darkness and calls it only the beginning of the end.

[00:03:13] He says “heat death” may be misleading because the end is cooler and darker: here heat refers to particles’ disordered motion. He points viewers to his video on distinguishing past from future and introduces entropy.

### G003 [00:03:32–00:05:00]

[00:03:32] Julius describes entropy in terms of disorder relative to an initial state. A completed puzzle has low entropy because there is only one way to construct it as a whole, whereas pieces can form a pile in many configurations. He qualifies that it is not quite that simple and says he will return to the example.

[00:03:54] He links entropy to higher temperature: ice molecules have a particular arrangement, while warmer liquid water permits freer motion, with steam extending the idea. He states that the second law of thermodynamics means entropy can only increase in an isolated system and can never be reversed; referring again to his earlier video, he says this process distinguishes past from future, and that things left long enough decay into disorder.

[00:04:30] He anticipates the objection that reassembling the puzzle reverses entropy: it decreases entropy in the puzzle system but ignores the rest of the universe. Digested food provides the assembler’s energy, fingers create friction, and breathing also increases entropy.

### G004 [00:05:02–00:06:36]

[00:05:02] Julius concludes that reassembling the puzzle does not break the second law when the entire universe is considered. He jokingly anticipates another objection: could one hide the increased entropy by throwing oneself into a black hole after finishing, since not even light escapes? He wishes the hypothetical person luck but says their death would be in vain: black holes have entropy too. Adding a person increases the hole’s mass, horizon size and surface area, where energy is emitted through Hawking radiation.

[00:05:47] He reiterates that even black holes eventually evaporate, leaving radiation spreading through an extremely dark universe whose expansion accelerates due to dark energy. Everything fades to darkness; no black holes survive heat death. He calls this ending dark, agonizing and perhaps disappointing, but says it entails maximum entropy and remarkable implications for time.

# How the END of the Universe RECREATES a New Universe

- Source: consolidated from timestamped transcript; NOT independently fact-checked

### G001 [00:00:00–00:01:48]

[00:00:00] Julius says a universe whose future is “plagued by the acceleration of dark matter,” the cosmological constant, evolves toward emptiness and darkness. Accelerating expansion creates more empty space and hence more dark energy in an unstoppable positive feedback loop. Eventually stars burn out and black holes decay, leaving only exponentially expanding space, or de Sitter space. He asks whether the universe truly ends and says the answer requires exploring entropy and the arrow of time.

[00:00:44] He introduces this as the final episode of his series on heat death, which he calls one of the most likely, arguably *the* most likely, ways the universe ends. The series also considers how heat death could lead to a new universe, perhaps identical to ours. Previous episodes explained accelerating expansion, distant galaxies beginning to disappear, and why the process is irreversible. Music marks the transition.

[00:01:26] He says burned-out stars, decaying particles and evaporating black holes convert matter into free radiation that spreads as heat, or pure disordered energy. Reduction to heat radiation maximizes entropy because energy flow is no longer restricted.

### G002 [00:01:50–00:03:24]

[00:01:50] Julius says one might expect expansion to dilute radiation and lower entropy along with temperature, but it does not. He cites Katie Mack, author of *The End of Everything*: under steady exponential expansion, an observer can define a true horizon beyond which nothing can ever reach them. Like a black hole’s horizon, it has entropy and temperature, but its heat goes inward rather than outward. Its temperature is about 10⁻⁴⁰ degrees above absolute zero; once everything else has decayed, this radiation contains all the universe’s entropy.

[00:02:42] In this pure de Sitter state, Julius says, the universe has maximum entropy; there is no way for its total **energy**, as he puts it, to increase, so the arrow of time is gone. Recalling the previous episode and another video, he says the arrow of time and second law of thermodynamics are essential: without further entropy increase, organized structures and evolution cannot exist. Anything happening requires energy moving between places, and energy gradients underpin all work.

### G003 [00:03:26–00:05:06]

[00:03:26] Julius describes the resulting universe as a huge, very cold heat bath, but says important exceptions change everything. At quantum scales, or larger scales after a *very* long wait—he jokes, not the kind of length some men ascribe to an organ—unpredictable fluctuations can randomly put parts of a system into a low-entropy state. He references another video that may hint at where his argument is heading.

[00:04:01] Larger systems are less likely to be affected by fluctuations, he says, but an eternally accelerating universe containing only a cosmological constant has ample time and space: any event with a nonzero probability, however small, will occur infinitely often given infinite time. A fully built piano spontaneously appearing in empty space is extraordinarily unlikely but possible in principle; by the same reasoning, a universe can and eventually must appear.

[00:04:53] He introduces Poincaré recurrence as a statistical-mechanics principle: any arrangement of particles in a system eventually returns to the same position, with less likely configurations taking longer.

### G004 [00:05:07–00:06:42]

[00:05:07] Continuing on recurrence, Julius says any state a system can occupy will recur infinitely often given infinite time, with recurrence time determined by its rarity. He attributes to physicists Anthony Aguirre, Sean Carroll and Matthew Johnson a calculation that, after about a trillion times the universe’s age, one could watch a piano randomly assemble in an empty box.

[00:05:33] He likens the post-heat-death universe to a giant box for fluctuations: if the Big Bang was a state it occupied and the subsequent universe lasts eternally, the Big Bang will recur infinitely often. He jokes that the viewer’s present moment, watching without subscribing or enabling notifications, can recur exactly as it is infinitely often.

[00:06:08] He calls the Big Bounce and Big Crunch unlikely, perhaps subjects for another video, but considers rebirth through heat death and fluctuations over infinite time “extremely realistic”; this may not be the first universe. He wonders whether exact consciousness could be recreated so one lives again, or whether, like uploading consciousness to a computer, it would merely make a copy while the original dies forever.

### G005 [00:06:45–00:08:18]

[00:06:45] Julius says he does not know the answer about consciousness, would like to explore it in a future philosophy video and will return to it. He says Nietzsche considered this possibility before knowing it was physically possible and before heat death was known; the philosopher might have been right.

[00:07:06] He presents the Boltzmann brain problem: it would be much more likely for one’s exact brain, memories and abilities to appear spontaneously in a closed, safe environment in random space and imagine this precise scenario than for an entire Big Bang to occur, because the latter requires even lower entropy. On that probability argument, he says, it is more likely that we live in a simulation. He has never liked simulation theory as normally framed—an intentionally created program—which he calls stupid because no glitches have ever been recorded; this Boltzmann-brain version, however, strikes him as reasonable.

[00:07:51] Nevertheless, Julius says he and many physicists and cosmologists disagree with the Boltzmann-brain conclusion: despite its requiring a smaller entropy change, a Big Bang might be more likely. Some cosmologists argue a de Sitter universe is more likely to create a low-entropy state like the Big Bang than something small on the brink of reabsorption. Their argument, he says, is that recreating such a state may seem to require substantial quantum-fluctuation energy but actually removes only a little total entropy from the whole system.

### G006 [00:08:21–00:10:09]

[00:08:21] Julius notes that other cosmologists disagree, so we may never know whether this is a simulation. He personally favors recurrence of a low-entropy Big Bang, qualifies his own opinion and invites comments.

[00:08:43] Assuming that perspective is accurate, he reiterates his central question: when the same Big Bang recreates the universe infinitely often, is our consciousness perfectly recreated so we unknowingly relive the same life, or is it merely a copy, as with uploading consciousness? Either way, he finds hope in the possibility that we could live again and perhaps already have infinitely often without knowing it. The supposed physical possibility gives him hope; if he must live the same life infinitely often, he intends to live his best possible life and hopes viewers do too.

[00:09:35] He closes the series on how the universe ends and perhaps restarts, asks viewers to subscribe and enable notifications, and music plays. A final “you” is heard at [00:10:09].

# How the Universe ENDS and RESTARTS - Heat Death

- Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=8IgjE-19FeM
- Published (UTC): 2022-09-02T20:52:09+00:00
- Source: consolidated from timestamped transcript; NOT independently fact-checked

### G001 [00:00:00–00:01:31]

[00:00:00] Julius introduces heat death as one of the most likely, arguably the most likely, endings of the universe, and says it might lead to a new universe precisely like ours. He intends to cover alternatives—the big crunch, big rip, vacuum decay and big bounce—in future videos.

[00:00:24] He previews concepts needed to understand heat death, including a distant region where the farther away an object is, the larger it appears, contrary to everyday experience.

[00:00:47] Julius recounts that Einstein published general relativity without a cosmological constant in 1915, then added one in 1917 because his equations implied a dynamic universe, whereas he and many others believed it was static. He says Belgian astrophysicist Georges Lemaître combined relativity with Hubble’s recent findings to show expansion in 1927, and Einstein accepted expansion in 1931, calling the constant one of his biggest mistakes, alongside his letter to Roosevelt. Julius blames Einstein for neither, saying his heart was in the right place.

### G002 [00:01:34–00:03:11]

[00:01:34] Julius says that in 1917 the big bang was not widely accepted, Hubble’s expansion findings and the cosmic background radiation discovery were still ahead, and a steady-state universe was arguable. He points viewers to another video about the competing theories and what came before the big bang.

[00:01:53] He says Einstein introduced the cosmological constant to prevent gravity from drawing stars together and collapsing the universe: although nothing in the universe seemed able to counter gravity, perhaps space itself could. The equation worked for a static universe, but expansion instead could counter gravity, even if gravity eventually slowed, stopped and reversed it.

[00:02:26] Julius cites Hubble’s use of galaxy redshift to show expansion and says its accelerating rate makes a big crunch unlikely. Although Einstein had been embarrassed by the constant, Julius says the 1998 Supernova Cosmology Project results suggested he might have been partially right to include it.

### G003 [00:03:12–00:04:46]

[00:03:12] Julius says the Supernova Cosmology Project found expansion accelerating rather than slowing because of the cosmological constant, which may represent 70% of the universe’s total mass-energy density; the High-Z Supernova Search Team announced the same result. He says the constant works mathematically but is not necessarily considered a rational solution: nothing explains why it exists or has its particular value. Addressing a possible connection to quantum fluctuations from his prior video, he says quantum-field-theory calculations would yield a value 120 orders of magnitude larger.

[00:03:55] He defines dark energy broadly as any hypothesized phenomenon that could accelerate expansion. Whatever caused initial cosmic inflation eventually switched off, he says, but dark energy remains. He attributes its initially lesser effect to densely packed matter and little intervening space; as expansion separated matter, dark energy became more influential, creating a positive feedback loop of accelerating expansion.

### G004 [00:04:48–00:06:27]

[00:04:48] Julius says that about six billion years ago ordinary cosmic inflation had diffused matter enough for the cosmological constant or dark energy to become noticeable. Showing his chart, he jokes, “Shut up, I’m not an artist.” He says exponential acceleration probably leads to heat death and maximum entropy, after which time would cease to exist because there would be no matter to “ban” space-time; he teases something interesting that might then occur.

[00:05:29] Citing Katie Mack’s *The End of Everything*, he says measurements of supernova explosions from before acceleration began let us trace the preceding deceleration and approximate transition. Dark energy might not be a new dynamic field, he adds, because a cosmological constant fits the data perfectly. Ironically, Einstein’s proposed safeguard against collapse might bring doom through expansion and heat death instead.

[00:06:04] He asks viewers to subscribe and enable notifications for the next episode, reiterating the possibility that the universe could restart exactly as it is now. He then begins an E-Deals membership promotion.

### G005 [00:06:28–00:08:07]

[00:06:28] Julius says E-Deals membership is available for a limited period for $14.99 via the description; its website has the details. He promotes potential monthly savings of hundreds of dollars through free food, heavily discounted orders, free Amazon products, monitors and release information, among other benefits.

[00:06:55] He describes a dark-energy apocalypse as slow and agonizing: isolation, loneliness, emptiness and a fade to black. In his account, the cosmological constant ends everything *within* the universe rather than the universe itself, and accelerated expansion never stops once begun.

[00:07:18] A new episode repeats the series introduction and the possibility of heat death producing an identical universe. After recapping the previous explanation of accelerating expansion, Julius introduces the observable universe and defines its particle horizon as the farthest distance observable even with the most advanced instruments, limited by light speed and the universe’s age.

### G006 [00:08:09–00:09:41]

[00:08:09] Julius explains that light takes time to travel, so more distant objects are seen further in the past. He defines the particle horizon as the distance from which light emitted at the first instant would take the universe’s entire age to reach us.

[00:08:30] Although the universe is 13.8 billion years old, he says a particle-horizon radius of 13.8 billion light-years would assume a static universe. He reiterates that expansion has continued throughout its history, with cosmic inflation responsible for much of it before “passing the ball” to dark energy six billion years ago. Thus something close enough to send us light 13.8 billion years ago is now over 45 billion light-years away, and the observable universe is approximately a 45-billion-light-year-radius sphere centered on us.

[00:09:24] He says the cosmic microwave background is the closest we can get to seeing that edge and refers to another video, noting that its discovery was key to verifying big bang claims. He then begins saying we can see galaxies now “over 30…”; the statement is cut off in the excerpt.

### G007 [00:09:44–00:11:14]

[00:09:44] Continuing a distance given as “billion light years away,” Julius says it is much closer than the edge of the particle horizon. Light from those galaxies began traveling toward us before the galaxies reached such great distances; otherwise it would not have had enough time to arrive.

[00:10:01] He says that in an expanding, accelerating universe, more distant objects recede faster, and beyond a certain distance a galaxy recedes faster than light can catch up. Although nothing can move faster than light, he distinguishes a galaxy moving through space from the space between objects expanding: their separation can grow faster than light, albeit at a speed he describes as fairly close to it.

[00:10:51] Reiterating how such objects can be visible, he says their light left long ago, when the universe was significantly smaller and there was less distance to cover despite continuing expansion.

### G008 [00:11:17–00:12:46]

[00:11:17] Julius says the light eventually “caught up,” as expansion slowed, reaching a region where recession was slower than light. Citing Katie Mack, author of *The End of Everything*, he describes it as entering our Hubble radius from outside.

[00:11:34] His analogy is a person running at top speed on a treadmill moving faster than they can run: they fall gradually behind, but if they stay on it and a bad motor slows the treadmill, they can catch up to the front and reach their destination. In a hypothetical universe with slowing expansion, increasingly distant objects would become visible over time.

[00:12:19] He says dark energy “ruins all the fun”: our expansion is accelerating, not slowing, and has done so for the past six billion years since cosmic inflation “handed the ball off” to dark energy, as shown in a prior episode’s chart. Though the Hubble radius is growing, he says it grows too slowly to prevent the loss of previously visible objects.

### G009 [00:12:48–00:14:14]

[00:12:48] Julius says that as the Hubble radius grows, we see nothing new, only regain what expansion made us lose. Eventually only Andromeda will remain visible among other galaxies: it is moving toward us and is close enough for gravity to counter expansion, and it will have collided with our galaxy. He attributes Andromeda’s different color from other galaxies to redshifting, a subject he may cover in a full video.

[00:13:19] Returning to an earlier claim, he says objects appear smaller with increasing distance over a great range, but beyond a point the relationship reverses. He calls this useful to astronomers because very distant objects appear larger than they actually are. His explanation parallels visibility of faster-than-light-receding objects: the light now reaching us left when its source was much closer, and the further back in time, the smaller the universe and the shorter the distance light had to travel.

### G010 [00:14:16–00:15:58]

[00:14:16] Julius calls the apparent contradiction of familiar reality fascinating but says it spells very bad news for the universe’s future, to be explored next episode. He asks viewers to subscribe and enable notifications, share the video—especially with a drunk friend, whose expression he jokes will be priceless—and like it if they enjoyed or learned from it. He recommends Katie Mack’s *The End of Everything*, linked in the description, and signs off wishing viewers a good day and telling them to stay skeptical and curious.

[00:14:59] A new episode begins: Julius asks why dark energy must be so cruel. He compares galaxies fading from view through accelerated expansion to an ancient photograph deteriorating. After the Milky Way and Andromeda collide, even the local group will eventually become invisible, leaving us isolated in darkness; he calls this merely the beginning of the end. Music follows.

[00:15:44] He introduces the series as explaining heat death, one of the most likely—and arguably the most likely—ends of the universe, and how it could lead to a new universe, perhaps precisely like ours.

### G011 [00:16:00–00:17:42]

[00:16:00] Julius says prior episodes laid groundwork for heat death by explaining accelerating expansion and the resulting disappearance of distant galaxies. He calls this episode’s subject the darkest yet.

[00:16:23] In an account he attributes to Katie Mack, each dying super-galaxy will become isolated, with no fresh gas arriving to fuel stars. Existing stars will burn out, exploding as supernovae or, more often, shedding outer layers and becoming slow-burning relics that cool over billions or trillions of years. Black holes will grow for a time: some will swallow galaxies’ worth of dead stellar remnants, while others will stop growing because no matter comes close enough. Once the stars have faded, ultimate decay sets in.

[00:16:59] Julius says black holes too evaporate. Although most initially believed them eternal, Stephen Hawking calculated in the 1970s that quantum effects at their horizons make them glow, drawing energy and causing mass loss. Evaporation starts slowly, accelerates and ends in an explosion and disappearance after an extremely long lifetime; even massive galactic-center black holes eventually fade. He adds that the matter of planets and stars will also decay if left long enough.

### G012 [00:17:45–00:19:16]

[00:17:45] Julius says most matter particles are unstable, giving a neutron decaying into a proton, electron and antineutrino as an example. He mentions an estimate of over 10³³ years, after which even hydrogen atoms, the universe’s most abundant, will decay. He blames dark energy for the slow fade to darkness, while saying that fade is only the beginning of the end.

[00:18:13] He says “heat death” may mislead because the end is cooler and darker: here, heat means disordered particle motion. Referring to his video on distinguishing past and future, he introduces entropy as disorder relative to an initial state. A completed puzzle has low entropy because there is one particular way to assemble it; its pieces in a pile can have many configurations and still be a pile. He qualifies that the matter is not quite so simple and promises to return to the example.

[00:18:54] He links entropy with higher temperature: ice molecules are arranged in a particular order, liquid water’s move more freely and water is warmer; he extends the idea to steam. He says the key takeaway is that, under the second law of thermodynamics, entropy can only increase in an isolated system; his sentence continues beyond the excerpt.

### G013 [00:19:18–00:20:47]

[00:19:18] Julius says the process of decay into disorder distinguishes past from future. Reassembling a puzzle reduces that system’s entropy, but not the universe’s: the person uses energy from digested food, causes friction by gripping pieces, and creates entropy by breathing. Thus, he says, the second law of thermodynamics remains unbroken when the whole universe is considered.

[00:20:06] He jokingly considers throwing oneself into a black hole after completing the puzzle to dispose of the increased entropy, since even light cannot escape. Wishing the hypothetical person luck, he says the death would be in vain: black holes have entropy, and adding a person increases the hole’s mass, horizon size and surface area, where energy is emitted through Hawking radiation.

### G014 [00:20:49–00:22:39]

[00:20:49] Julius concludes that even black holes evaporate, leaving radiation spreading through a dark universe whose expansion accelerates due to dark energy. Everything eventually fades to darkness; nothing, including black holes, survives heat death. He calls this ending dark, agonizing and perhaps disappointing, but says maximum entropy has remarkable implications for time. He previews an argument that the universe could be recreated precisely as it is now, including the viewer watching and perhaps subscribing.

[00:21:41] After music, a new episode begins: Julius describes a future “plagued by the acceleration of dark matter,” the cosmological constant. He says accelerating expansion produces more empty space and therefore more dark energy in an unstoppable positive feedback loop. Stars burn out, black holes decay, and only exponentially expanding space—“decenter space”—remains. He asks whether this means the universe truly ends and introduces entropy and the arrow of time.

[00:22:28] Following music, he introduces the multipart series’ heat-death scenario as one of the most likely, arguably the most likely, endings, and says it may lead to a new universe.

### G015 [00:22:42–00:24:22]

[00:22:42] Julius adds that the new universe might be precisely like ours. He recaps earlier episodes on accelerating expansion, distant galaxies beginning to disappear, and why the process is irreversible, and identifies this as the final episode. Music follows.

[00:23:13] He says a star burning out, a particle decaying or a black hole evaporating converts matter into free radiation, which spreads as heat—pure disordered energy. Once something becomes heat radiation, he says, its entropy is maximized because energy flow is unrestricted. Although expansion might seem to dilute the radiation and lower entropy with temperature, he says this does not happen.

[00:23:44] Citing Katie Mack, author of *The End of Everything*, he explains that steady exponential expansion gives an observer a true horizon beyond which nothing can ever reach them. Like a black-hole horizon, it has entropy and temperature, but its heat goes inward rather than outward. Its temperature is approximately 10⁻⁴⁰ degrees above absolute zero.

### G016 [00:24:24–00:25:58]

[00:24:24] Continuing the explanation attributed to Mack, Julius says that after everything else decays, horizon radiation contains all the universe’s entropy. A pure de Sitter universe has maximum entropy; from then on, he says, its total **energy** cannot increase, so in a real sense the arrow of time is gone.

[00:24:43] Referring back to earlier explanations, he says the arrow of time and second law are essential: without increasing entropy, organized structures and evolution cannot exist. Things require energy to move and gradients to perform work, but these cannot exist in what is essentially a huge, very cold heat bath.

[00:25:17] He introduces consequential exceptions: at quantum scales, or larger scales given a very long wait, unpredictable fluctuations can randomly shift parts of a system into low-entropy states. He jokes that “very long” is not the kind of length some men claim for an organ, and refers viewers to another video. The larger the system, he says, the less likely fluctuations are to affect it, but an eternally accelerating universe containing only a cosmological constant has ample time and space.

### G017 [00:26:00–00:27:38]

[00:26:00] Julius says any event with a probability, however small, will occur infinitely many times given infinite time. A fully built piano spontaneously appearing in empty space is extremely unlikely but possible in principle; by the same reasoning, a universe could spontaneously appear and, given infinite time, must eventually do so.

[00:26:39] He describes Poincaré recurrence as the statistical-mechanics principle that any arrangement of particles eventually returns to the same configuration, with rarer configurations taking longer. With infinite time, he says, every possible state recurs infinitely often. He attributes to physicists Anthony Aguirre, Sean Carroll and Matthew Johnson a calculation that, after roughly a trillion times the universe’s age, a piano could randomly assemble in an empty box.

[00:27:20] He likens the post-heat-death universe to one giant box for fluctuations: if the Big Bang was a state the universe once occupied and the post-heat-death universe lasts eternally, he argues, that state will recur infinitely often.

### G018 [00:27:40–00:29:16]

[00:27:40] Julius says the exact present moment could recur infinitely, joking that the viewer is still watching without subscribing or enabling notifications. He considers the Big Bounce and Big Crunch unlikely and might make a video explaining why, but calls rebirth through heat death and random fluctuations over infinite time “extremely realistic”; this may not be the first universe.

[00:28:17] He wonders whether one’s precise consciousness could be recreated so that one lives again, or whether it would be like uploading consciousness to a computer: a copy exists while the original dies forever. He does not know, would like to explore it in a philosophy video, and says he will return to it. He says Nietzsche considered the possibility before knowing it was physically possible and before heat death was known, and might have been right.

[00:28:52] Julius says it is far more likely that one’s exact brain, with its memories and abilities, spontaneously appears in a closed, safe environment in random space—or imagines this precise scenario—because a whole Big Bang would require even lower entropy. He concludes that, according to probability, it is more likely that “we live in a simulation”; his next personal remark is cut off.

### G019 [00:29:19–00:30:53]

[00:29:19] Julius says he has never been a big fan of simulation theory. It is rarely explained in the manner he has described; instead, it is usually presented as an intentionally created program, which he considers stupid because no glitches have ever been recorded. He considers the Boltzmann brain problem reasonable, but disagrees with it, as do many physicists and cosmologists.

[00:29:42] Despite the lower change in entropy required for the alternative, he says a Big Bang might be much more likely. Some cosmologists argue that a de Sitter universe is more likely to create a low-entropy state like the Big Bang than something small on the brink of reabsorption: recreating that state may appear to require much quantum-fluctuation energy, but might remove only a little of the system’s total entropy. Other cosmologists disagree, so, he says, we may never truly know whether this is a simulation. He favors recurrence of a low-entropy state like the Big Bang, but asks what his opinion matters and invites comments.

[00:30:30] Assuming that perspective is accurate and the universe is recreated through the exact same Big Bang infinitely many times, his biggest remaining question is whether consciousness is also perfectly recreated or merely copied: can we live our exact same lives again without knowing it, or is it just a copy, as with uploading consciousness to a computer?

### G020 [00:30:54–00:31:55]

[00:30:54] Whatever the answer, Julius finds hope in the possibility that we could live again, and perhaps already have infinitely many times without knowing it. The fact that he considers this physically possible gives him hope; if he must live the same life infinitely often, he intends to live his best possible life and hopes viewers do too.

[00:31:22] He closes “How the Universe Ends and Perhaps Restarts,” asks viewers to subscribe and enable notifications, and music plays, followed by a final “you.”

# TikTok and Psychological Warfare - Explained

- Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=HX1Z_NyQrMo
- Published (UTC): 2022-09-04T20:45:21+00:00
- Source: consolidated from timestamped transcript; NOT independently fact-checked

### G001 [00:00:00–00:01:43]

[00:00:00] Julius suspects viewers have seen other videos on TikTok’s ramifications, yet says most “still haven’t downloaded.” He mockingly asks whether their self-awareness makes them immune to the algorithm or merely another statistic. Perhaps, he suggests, it is already too late: in three years they may have changed friends, alienated others and formed a new identity. He calls what is happening to impressionable minds deliberate and the most elaborate psychological warfare strategy any nation has faced.

[00:00:43] He says India and Afghanistan banned TikTok; Pakistan repeatedly banned and reinstated it; Bangladesh and Indonesia also banned it in the past; and a near-permanent US ban was revoked under Biden. He quotes Biden calling it a “matter of genuine concern” that a Chinese operation had access to over 100 million young people, particularly in America. Julius says TikTok is presented as a major Western cyberthreat because it collects more information than other social media, but its algorithm’s psychological impact receives less discussion.

[00:01:30] He says parent company ByteDance bought Musical.ly for $1 billion in November 2017, resulting in TikTok’s launch in September 2017, and that TikTok recently surpassed one billion users.

### G002 [00:01:46–00:03:24]

[00:01:46] Julius finds a billion users frightening against a world population of fewer than eight billion. An inserted news voice says BuzzFeed obtained internal TikTok and ByteDance communications, including one saying “everything can be seen in China,” and that a TikTok letter to senators indicated information was going back to Beijing.

[00:02:18] Julius cites FCC commissioner Brendan Carr’s letter urging Apple and Google to remove TikTok: Carr describes Beijing-based ByteDance as beholden to the Chinese Communist Party and legally required to comply with Chinese surveillance demands. Emphasizing “required,” Julius adds that TikTok’s privacy policy promises not to sell personal information to third parties but reserves internal use for business development. He considers user information more vulnerable there than on other social media.

[00:02:57] He says privacy and surveillance are serious but familiar warnings; he raises them primarily to establish TikTok and ByteDance’s close connection to China and specifically the CCP. He notes that conflict between capitalist and communist ideologies, propaganda and psychological warfare are not new.

### G003 [00:03:27–00:05:03]

[00:03:27] Julius calls the apparently innocent app a major psychological warfare weapon and says ByteDance whistleblowers have exposed deliberate, frequent censorship. He claims TikTok’s algorithm differs completely from that of Douyin, the Chinese version—whose name he translates as “shaking sound”—and says TikTok itself cannot be downloaded in China.

[00:03:56] He contrasts Western TikTok’s alleged promotion of “degeneracy” with Douyin’s positive promotion of productivity, nuclear families and achievement. He says Western users see mental illness treated as a quirky identity, cheating and single parenthood celebrated, and girls dancing provocatively to promote OnlyFans; Chinese users instead see hard work and the value of nuclear families. He calls the nuclear family a foundation of stable civilization, citing multiple studies, and says Douyin never promotes the other videos.

[00:04:43] He argues that contaminating minds outside China destroys nations from within and intensifies divisions, but says destruction is only one part of the threat; another is the promotion of communist ideologies.

### G004 [00:05:06–00:06:51]

[00:05:06] Julius says Douyin’s “positive energy” section overtly promotes the CCP, while the party’s presence on ordinary TikTok is immense but subtler. He cites reported figures: support for socialism rose by 10 during the pandemic; 30% of Gen Z and 27% of millennials view Marxism favorably; and 74% of Gen Z and 70% of millennials do not see Marxism as a totalitarian state suppressing citizens’ freedom. He contrasts these figures with America’s decades as a center of anti-communism.

[00:05:48] A news insert describes students losing patience after more than a month confined at home, people crying for help from windows, police kicking in a woman’s door after she refused quarantine, robots reminding people to mask, poor central-quarantine conditions and people forced from their homes.

[00:06:15] Julius cites a report that 26% of Americans, including 35% of millennials and 31% of Gen Z, support gradually replacing capitalism with a more socialist system. He says these shifts and TikTok’s meteoric rise occurred in the same recent years. Acknowledging other factors, he argues they combine with the growing algorithm to create a feedback loop: more people post communist ideas, the algorithm promotes them, more users see them and then post similar videos.

### G005 [00:06:53–00:08:18]

[00:06:53] Completing the feedback-loop account, Julius calls it heavily lopsided and deliberately controlled by the CCP. He says the frightening aspect of this psychological warfare is that it taps directly into the brain’s automatic portion.

[00:07:10] He introduces a clip from his earlier video about the implicit association test, or IAT, and why people fail it. In that clip, Julius says the test is effective because years of stored experience cannot consciously be set aside. For doubters who might fear other tests, he offers a flowers-versus-insects IAT, linked in that video’s description courtesy of the creators of *Blindspot*, predicting that most results will show a preference for flowers.

[00:08:02] In the clip, he says surprising results arise because the mind has reflective and automatic facets. Reflective preferences are well known to us, such as religious beliefs, and can include complex judgments; he begins an example of choosing between presidential candidates.

### G006 [00:08:21–00:09:48]

[00:08:21] Continuing the earlier-video clip, Julius gives the example of voting for President B as better for the country despite personally benefiting more from President A. He attributes to psychologist William James the idea that conscious thoughts and feelings provide fuel for action; religious belief, for instance, can lead someone to pray or enlist to defend a religious state.

[00:08:44] He contrasts the automatic mind, which he calls almost a stranger, saying implicit thoughts and feelings also affect actions and can produce surprising IAT results. He calls bias against a group one belongs to mentally or physically “dissociation,” referring to two examples at the start of the earlier video. He says biracial Malcolm Gladwell, whose beloved mother is Jamaican, was shocked and disturbed by his results, and claims such reactions are common.

[00:09:26] Julius argues that this unfamiliar part of the mind is beyond one’s control, so people believe ideas are entirely their own without realizing the CCP has skewed the positive feedback loop in its favor. He says TikTok and ByteDance’s CCP bias is impossible to deny, then begins addressing viewers who think TikTok cannot affect them.

### G007 [00:09:49–00:11:32]

[00:09:49] Julius moves from whether TikTok can change political views to other possible influences. Reiterating his earlier claim that TikTok celebrates mental illness and thereby destroys society, he says its algorithm heavily promotes a self-diagnosis trend and that multiple such videos can be found within minutes on the home or For You page.

[00:10:20] He says teenage girls have been seeking medical help for tics, including jerky movements and verbal outbursts, at up to ten times the pre-COVID-19 rate. Citing an October 19 *Wall Street Journal* report, he says initially baffled movement-disorder doctors in the US, Canada, Australia and UK compared cases and found that many girls had watched TikTok influencers with Tourette syndrome. Texas Children’s Hospital reported approximately 60 cases since March 2020, versus one or two annually before the pandemic.

[00:11:17] Julius cites a July 2021 *Movement Disorders Clinical Practice* paper reporting that 19 of the 28 most popular influencers with the condition said they developed new tics after watching other creators. He begins its conclusion, continued in the next group.

### G008 [00:11:34–00:13:10]

[00:11:34] Julius quotes the paper’s conclusion that “TikTok tics” differ from typical Tourette syndrome presentations but share many characteristics with functional tics, and that the authors believe them to be an example of mass sociogenic illness: behaviors, emotions or conditions spreading spontaneously through a group. He urges viewers to reread that last sentence.

[00:11:53] He says some affected girls said “beans” in a British accent, as does a famous British TikToker who frequently posts videos of her tics. He claims severe Tourette’s tics are spreading from influencers to users, and that some influencers fake illness for attention and donations. He argues that if such tics can spread, a milder political perspective could infiltrate the brain’s automatic portion in the same way.

[00:12:29] Returning to his promised explanation, Julius claims that, beyond the alleged societal destruction caused by celebrating mental illness, a further sinister reason also explains the algorithm’s favoring of gender ideology and critical race theory. He says these and mental illnesses have in common groups that perceive themselves as oppressed out-groups, invoking Marxism. He argues that perceived victimhood in marginalized groups, the human desire for belonging, and people’s need for direction and purpose together can provoke uprisings, a thought completed in the next group.

### G009 [00:13:12–00:14:56]

[00:13:12] Julius quotes Mark R. Levin’s *American Marxism*: mass movements consume individual identity and uniqueness while assigning group identities based on race, age, income and similar categories to draw class distinctions. In the passage, demagogues invoke the welfare of the whole people while dividing them and driving them in directions needed to collapse an existing society or rule a new one.

[00:13:49] Julius claims TikTok’s promotion of content about mental illness, gender theory, critical race theory and other groups claiming marginalization or oppression “kills two birds with one stone”: it harms society from within, as he says he described earlier, and uses a Marxist tactic of group identity to provoke uprisings. He says it fosters “us versus them,” turning citizens against one another under the guise of social justice and progression.

[00:14:22] He quotes Levin describing a receptive audience for mass movements among the disenchanted, disaffected, dissatisfied and maladjusted, who are unwilling or unable to take responsibility for their real or perceived conditions and instead blame their surroundings, the system and others. Julius interprets this as an escape from accountability for misfortune, allowing someone to explain why their life is low quality.

### G010 [00:14:58–00:16:37]

[00:14:58] Continuing the Levin quotation, Julius says such people are drawn by false hopes and promises of utopian transformation and by criticism of a society to which they have a tentative or nonexistent connection. He reiterates that TikTok’s algorithm is intentionally designed this way and that the Chinese version’s algorithm is completely different.

[00:15:18] In conclusion, Julius recaps his claims: TikTok and ByteDance have close ties to the Chinese Communist Party, presenting a major user privacy threat and establishing a relationship and incentive; the algorithm’s design is deliberate, and China does not allow its citizens to use this version. He says CCP bias is obvious in the Chinese version’s “positive energy” section and more subtle in the regular version’s suppression and promotion of content.

[00:15:59] He recaps his argument that a politically biased algorithm can strongly influence users through the brain’s automatic portion. He presents Tourette’s as an extreme example intended to show that, if content can have that much influence, it can also influence something as minor as political perspective. He again says the promoted content both divides and destroys a nation from within and uses Marxist tactics.

### G011 [00:16:40–00:18:07]

[00:16:40] Julius calls ByteDance’s TikTok a propaganda machine and the greatest psychological-warfare weapon any nation has faced. He claims it is extremely addictive and more harmful to the frontal cortex than any other social-media app encountered.

[00:16:57] He advertises E-Deals membership for $14.99, available for a limited period through the description link, with details on its website. He says it can save hundreds of dollars monthly through free food, heavily discounted orders, free Amazon products, monitors, release information and more.

[00:17:26] Julius says this is only the beginning and children are growing up indoctrinated by TikTok’s algorithm. He finds it “insane” that TikTok has not been banned in the US and hints at suspicions about why an executive order to ban it was revoked: he compares it to knowingly letting a football player taking performance-enhancing drugs play temporarily to score points, despite the trouble when caught. He says that is not the video’s purpose, reiterates his psychological-warfare conclusion, and invites viewers to subscribe and enable notifications for thought-provoking content.
