# So you think you're unique? - Mimetic Theory

- Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=UdwcKO_hzto
- Published (UTC): 2022-10-06T18:38:50+00:00
- Source: consolidated from timestamped transcript; NOT independently fact-checked

### G001 [00:00:00–00:02:27]

- [00:00:00] Music accompanies an opening voice saying, “I can’t change things here,” “I can’t have an effect,” and “I don’t care what happens to me.”
- [00:00:44] Julius addresses people who see themselves as unique outliers at work, university, or among friends while others follow mainstream ideologies: they are just like everyone else.
- [00:01:08] Daily choices range from outfits to political beliefs. Julius refers to his separate video arguing free will is an illusion, but says today’s subject affects choices whether or not viewers agree. He introduces René Girard, author of *Things Hidden Since the Foundation of the World*, and his concept of mimetic desire.
- [00:01:42] A person might explain buying a shirt through preferences for its color, fit, or brand values, thereby claiming an independent decision uninfluenced by others. Girard noticed that classical literary protagonists typically wanted, to some degree, to become another accomplished person; Julius says everyone does likewise. Advertisers understand this and pay celebrities and influential people large sums for brand deals.

### G002 [00:02:28–00:04:01]

- [00:02:28] Julius says imitation can come from friends, parents, or even a small YouTuber with a few hundred subscribers, adding a joking request to help him out. He quotes Girard: “Man is the creature who does not know what to desire; he turns to others in order to make up his mind.” People desire what others desire because they imitate them.
- [00:02:51] Imitation is obvious when everybody wears Yeezys, but Julius says even a rebel deliberately choosing an underappreciated, low-key brand imitates contrarianism, perhaps learned from a movie or YouTuber. Mimetic desire is inescapable; trying harder to deviate makes it more paradoxical, since one knows one is not the only contrarian.
- [00:03:35] An illustrative dialogue clip has one person accuse another of needing to be in the out-group, opposing whoever is powerful or successful, and wanting to feel like the smartest person in the room. The accused protests, then calls *Titanic* horrible and *Slumdog Millionaire* overrated and terrible; the exchange turns to *Cocktail*.

### G003 [00:04:03–00:05:45]

- [00:04:03] The dialogue clip continues: the accused calls *Cocktail* “not a bad film” and one of its era’s best examples of classically structured cinema; the other responds, “You make me sick, Brian.” Julius returns to the example of admiring a movie character who sets himself apart from the in-crowd.
- [00:04:19] Julius extends mimetic desire beyond fashion to finance, calling the dot-com and housing bubbles epitomes of it. He argues that even contrarians who benefited, such as Michael Burry, experienced it: Burry began learning finance from information he encountered, and exposure combined with genetics predisposed him toward shorting mortgage-backed securities. Julius speculates about books, genetically influenced attraction to ideas, or a contrarian father or professor, explicitly saying he does not know but believes the influence had to come from somewhere.
- [00:05:11] He says mimetic desire explains fights over trivial things and competition for the same jobs, auctioned art, or girlfriend; citing Girard, he reiterates that imitation is inevitable and has no solution. In an increasingly divided society, consciously or subconsciously adopted imitation can profoundly affect life: controversial opinions can create or destroy friendships, cost a job, and damage or help a reputation.

### G004 [00:05:47–00:07:30]

- [00:05:50] Julius may make a video on cancel culture, which he calls destructive and reminiscent of Marxism. He presents it as an epitome of imitation: people gravitate toward political correctness and follow others “like sheep,” whether they genuinely agree or not, because otherwise they may lose careers and friends. Some fake beliefs to fit in, and their doing so expands the influence of those cultural ideas in a positive feedback loop.
- [00:06:31] Julius describes a video in which an interviewer on a “heavily woke” campus described Andrew Tate’s actions, which many respondents liked, before naming Tate; Julius says their opinions then changed nearly 100 percent of the time. He says the overwhelming majority could give no reason for disliking him, and those who did often used a buzzword such as “misogynist” that they could not define. He suggests they absorbed a negative online atmosphere around the name and saw no reason to think critically when everyone around them agreed.
- [00:07:26] Julius qualifies that there are valid reasons both to dislike and to like Tate.

### G005 [00:07:33–00:09:17]

- [00:07:33] Julius says Tate often articulates his philosophies extremely, perhaps for entertainment, engagement, and virality, but that, broken down to fundamentals, a good majority are reasonable and agreeable in many cultures; he also acknowledges good arguments against some of them. His point is that the campus respondents reached definitive conclusions without critical thought: he calls that pure imitation.
- [00:08:03] An interview clip shows a person saying they dislike Tate, repeatedly questioning why the interviewer asks, and eventually explaining they have not seen much and do not seek his content because it does not interest them, but dislike everything they have seen. Asked whether they follow the media, the person says yes.
- [00:08:55] Julius says imitation works both ways: Tate’s admirers imitate his behavior and philosophies, and a website sells replicas of the Louis Vuitton glasses he wears. Reiterating that neither side escapes imitation, he argues that all organisms experience mimetic desire to some degree.

### G006 [00:09:20–00:10:47]

- [00:09:20] Julius compares people to a dog that ignores a toy until someone waves it and teases the dog with it; some dogs also chew sneakers because their owners wear them. He tells the viewer they are not uniquely special, but a product of exposure and genes, which create predispositions and alter the probabilistic outcomes of decisions.
- [00:09:46] Connecting this to his free-will video, he describes a decision as the dependent-variable sum of genetics and environmental factors such as books and videos. He says people cannot control exposure: a YouTube search itself results from prior circumstances—for example, being rejected by a girl and searching how to talk to girls—and viewers cannot control the search algorithm. Its suggestions and how far someone scrolls affect what they click.
- [00:10:34] Julius says this gives big tech considerable hidden power, a subject for another day. He recommends his free-will video, says he thinks viewers will enjoy it, and asks them to subscribe for more thought-provoking content.

### G007 [00:10:49–00:12:55]

- [00:10:49] Julius asks viewers to like the video or comment their notions. He says the description links to René Girard’s *Things Hidden Since the Foundation of the World*, which inspired the video and which he highly recommends. He wishes viewers a good day and says to stay curious and skeptical.
- [00:11:08] A different speaker discusses total conflict and starts to say it is automatically dealt with in a certain way, but leaves the thought unfinished. When people imitate not only their choice of opponent but also their feelings about everything, they gather against the same opponent. If someone is convinced one person is more guilty than the others, guilt emerges in their collective interplay; the process gains speed until one victim must be killed, driven out, or otherwise gotten rid of. He identifies this as what everyone calls the scapegoat.
- [00:12:24] The speaker says “scapegoat” comes from Tyndale’s English Bible translation. He contrasts terms in most European languages, transcribed as “emissary gold” and “emissary victim”: a victim sent out of the community or “scared.” He reiterates that the group unites against one person when everyone agrees that person is more of a culprit than the others.

# How Your BIRTHDAY Affects Your Life (Not Astrology)

- Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=2h9nkqaymwg
- Published (UTC): 2022-10-19T19:51:49+00:00
- Source: consolidated from timestamped transcript; NOT independently fact-checked

### G001 [00:00:00–00:02:15]

[00:00:00] Julius introduces the significance of birth month; music and applause follow, and he says, “thank you.”

[00:00:44] He says the video is not about astrology or anecdotal confirmation bias but will offer respectable data. Although birth month is outside one’s control, he claims it profoundly affects academics, athletics, career, relationships and mentality. The theme is positive feedback loops, illustrated by a snowball growing exponentially as it rolls down a snowy mountain.

[00:01:27] Using hockey as his first example, he says players’ birthdays show a bias toward earlier months. An NHL article discussed a PLOS ONE study suggesting the league’s draft favored players born earlier in the year. Julius says the data appear to support this, but he doubts the NHL is deliberately discriminating or would benefit from doing so. He begins citing the report’s draft statistics, completed in the next group.

### G002 [00:02:18–00:03:46]

[00:02:18] Julius completes the statistic: 36% of players drafted by NHL teams from 1980 through 2007 were born in January–March, versus 14.5% in the fourth quarter. He says such a consistent disparity is not coincidence and that the NHL article briefly connects it to selection while children are still developing.

[00:02:43] He argues that a few months make little difference between 17-year-olds, who have undergone most physical and mental growth, but can matter greatly when young children begin competitive sports. With a January cutoff in youth hockey and many other sports, two seven-year-olds can be in the same division even though one turns eight in January and the other in December. The older child is more likely to be physically larger and have more developed motor skills; genetics can make a younger child develop faster, but Julius calls that an outlier. In the bigger picture, he says, the older child’s advantages make better performance, perhaps even being best on the team, more likely.

### G003 [00:03:49–00:05:23]

[00:03:49] Julius asks why early-birth-month players remain overrepresented when developmental differences between 17-year-olds are negligible. He attributes this mainly to positive reinforcement: a top-performing child is encouraged to practice more, may receive special coaching attention and may be selected for elite teams with superior competition.

[00:04:26] He cites Malcolm Gladwell’s *Outliers* describing a self-fulfilling prophecy in Canadian hockey: the January 1 eligibility cutoff makes children born nearest it up to almost a year older than others in their age class. Canada takes hockey seriously, and coaches stream the best players into elite programs as early as eight or nine, offering more practice, games and better coaching; at eight, 10 or 11 extra months of maturity matters.

[00:05:12] Julius says the phenomenon occurs in many sports relative to their cutoff dates. He continues citing Gladwell, who says it is even more extreme in European soccer and US baseball and calls professional sports’ bias against children with the “wrong birthday” a bizarre, little-remarked fact.

### G004 [00:05:25–00:07:03]

[00:05:31] Julius says sports merely illustrate a phenomenon applicable to anything with age divisions, including school. Because cognitive ability develops with age, the oldest child in a class generally has an advantage; he reiterates that genetics also matter and asks viewers to consider large samples. He says many parents deliberately hold children back to obtain developmental advantages.

[00:06:06] He proposes that the feedback loop can shape a person beyond sports and academics: good grades may encourage the work ethic needed to sustain achievement and positive reinforcement, whereas bad grades may discourage it. That work ethic could carry into other areas, and academic outcomes could influence a future career—or whether someone has one. Hypothetically, a high-paying job versus no job could also produce very different relationships, or none. He qualifies these as extreme examples, with most people somewhere in between.

[00:06:55] He calls birth timing a significant, mostly ignored environmental factor. He contrasts frequent discussion of “wealth and equality” with an interrupted remark about birthdays, ending, “you got the point.”

### G005 [00:07:06–00:07:43]

[00:07:06] Julius says he believes genetics are often the most notable factor, but environment also matters. He calls this one of the most overlooked environmental factors and says a parent or guardian can control it to create a strategic positive feedback loop.

[00:07:22] He closes by asking viewers to subscribe, like or comment, recommends his video on free will, and says the description will link Gladwell’s *Outliers*, which inspired this video and which he highly recommends. He wishes viewers a great rest of their day.

# Why You Should Take The Black Pill - or shouldn't...

# Does Your Happiness Always Get Taken Away?

- Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Z6oaQzR7PDc
- Published (UTC): 2022-12-17T02:37:50+00:00
- Source: consolidated from timestamped transcript; NOT independently fact-checked

### G001 [00:00:00–00:01:54]

[00:00:00] Julius says everyone is the protagonist from their own perspective and usually sees themselves as the good hero deserving a happy ending, although they do not always get one. A subsequent voice says people do not perceive themselves as wrong, “all the heroes do not wear a cake,” and villains are made, not born: heroes and villains often have nearly identical beginnings, unlike their endings.

[00:00:35] Julius says misfortune prompts questions like “Why does everything bad happen to me?” and “What have I done to deserve this?” It can feel like a mystical spell when things keep going wrong and good fortune is snatched away. An anguished voice complains that happiness is taken away, that they cannot be happy and are reminded daily of what they cannot have because they are inadequate; people call them amazing and say their time will come, but they exclaim, “It’s always my motherfucking time, bitch.” One phrase is unclear: “I have to be missed.”

[00:01:23] Julius says this feeling occurs at work, school and in car accidents, but is most embodied in dating. He hypothesizes that dating is closest to life’s purpose of passing down genes for replication, citing Richard Dawkins’s description of organisms as genes’ “survival machines.” A Dawkins clip begins: genes, unlike DNA itself, are immortal; DNA turns over quickly.

### G002 [00:01:56–00:03:28]

[00:01:56] In the Dawkins clip, he says coded genetic information is potentially immortal, so the difference between successful and unsuccessful genes can matter for millions of years. Genes that persist are good at building bodies and controlling embryological processes to produce bodies capable of preserving and passing them on; he calls an individual body a “survival machine,” which he considers the most powerful way to interpret an organism.

[00:02:40] Julius offers to link his purpose-of-life video and invites alternative hypotheses for why the feeling occurs so often in dating, acknowledging he is unsure himself. Nevertheless, he says dating clearly amplifies the feeling that, as the good guy, one deserves a better plot and would get the girl in a fair world. Life is not a “blue-pilled Disney movie” where the genetically inferior nerd somehow gets the “Stacey”; he suggests such media may foster the expectation that good guys deserve the girl, but calls the thinking near-sighted. In species where females choose rather than dominant males fighting off subordinate males, he says, not all selection patterns revolve around survival advantage.

### G003 [00:03:33–00:05:08]

[00:03:33] Julius gives sexual selection in birds as an example: a long, colorful tail may be preferred even though a short tail is better for survival. He says Darwin could not comprehend why and assumed perhaps females simply liked the ornaments.

[00:03:49] Another explanatory voice describes Darwin’s theory as one of two main hypotheses: arbitrary beauty standards differ by species, and peahens choose large, bright, shiny, symmetrical feathers because they fancy them. A peahen choosing against that preference would have sons lacking the favored beauty genes, who would leave fewer offspring, creating a runaway positive-feedback loop called the “sexy son hypothesis.” The speaker jokes that evolutionary biologists love funny nicknames.

[00:04:42] Julius asks why a preference for particular colors or tail lengths would evolve without a survival advantage, and how natural selection could produce a seemingly random, useless feature. He says to think long-term: an organism’s purpose as a survival machine is to pass down genes, but merely surviving to pass them down once is insufficient if they are not passed on further.

### G004 [00:05:13–00:06:56]

[00:05:13] Julius asks what good a single offspring is if it never passes on its genes. He argues an organism can increase the chances of continuous replication by mating with a partner with ideal genetics, thereby making offspring sexually attractive. A colorful bird, for example, will have abundant reproductive success; attractive features need not confer survival advantages because they provide future reproductive advantage across generations.

[00:06:09] He applies this to humans, saying findings suggest all blue-eyed people descend from one ancestor born 6,000–10,000 years ago. He claims blue eyes had no survival advantage but spread to 8% of the world because their bearers were seen as more attractive and reproduced more successfully over time.

[00:06:46] Julius argues females do not deserve criticism for being overly selective: generally subconsciously, he says, they are looking out for their future offspring.

### G005 [00:06:59–00:08:35]

[00:06:59] Julius says he does not support offensive TikTok behavior toward genetically inferior men, but considers extreme female selectivity an aspect of nature. He claims females in most species are biologically programmed to be more selective because they invest more time, proteins and energy in offspring, while semen is abundant and eggs much more limited.

[00:07:36] He argues that a viewer with abundant choice would be equally selective, even as the supposed “good guy,” and asks whether that person was truly wronged by an unfair world or is simply encountering nature, which has winners and losers.

[00:08:05] Julius cites German researchers as finding that mothers have regularly outnumbered fathers in human history, meaning more women than men passed on DNA; he concludes there have been incels for thousands of years. He suggests standards may now be amplified by social media and by women’s ability to provide for themselves, which decreases the value of male provision and places more weight on genetic value. He calls this the most likely reason average height has increased in recent times, while reiterating that the fundamental aspect of nature has always been present.

### G006 [00:08:41–00:10:10]

[00:08:41] Julius finishes that nature’s pattern may be amplified today. He invokes elephant seals as an example of winners and losers on a sometimes horrific scale, while noting that they do not engage in concealed ovulation. Life is unfair, he says, but the viewer is not particularly cursed: not everyone wins, and people are survival machines trying to pass on genes.

[00:09:09] He argues that the probability a viewer is destined to be a loser in life is very low, though some will be; he says they cannot know for sure until they fully “looks max.” Before giving up, he recommends looks maxing, lean maxing and considering potential surgeries such as “air transplants,” as transcribed. Referring to his prior black-pill video, he says many use the black pill as a cop-out to quit and feel sorry for themselves without trying hardcore looks maxing. Life is unfair and becoming merely adequate might require much pain and suffering, but, he says, it is not necessarily impossible.

[00:09:51] Julius also approves of choosing healthy, fun “copes,” such as getting a pet, fishing or starting a business and creating a name and purpose for oneself, because they provide enjoyment. He strongly opposes completely giving up on life and expecting others to feel sorry for oneself, adding that someone always has it worse.

### G007 [00:10:12–00:10:48]

[00:10:12] Julius says viewers at least have their vision to watch the video and fingers and hands, joking that perhaps they could use them to like and subscribe.

[00:10:20] Seriously, he says life is unfair: some play on “Federer difficulty,” while Chads and Staceys live on recruit mode. Nevertheless, he says, it is not impossible to win or at least enjoy playing.

[00:10:36] He asks viewers to subscribe for more thought-provoking content, like and comment, and recommends his video on the purpose of life. He signs off, wishing them a fantastic rest of their day.

# The Future of Inequality

[00:00:00] Julius says the Pareto distribution illustrates that present income inequality will grow more extreme. Unequal quality of food, water, transportation, education, housing and safety is only the tip of the iceberg.

[00:00:35] He describes scientific advances as progressing exponentially, particularly genetic engineering. He says single-gene mutations associated with diabetes, cancer, Alzheimer’s and more can already be identified. Prospective IVF parents might want to alter their children’s germline to eliminate a Mendelian disorder, provide immunity to deadly viruses, reduce later cognitive decline or confer an advantage such as exceptionally strong bones.

[00:01:18] Julius says gene editing is not currently safe but will be, and that an optimal future for offspring can already be pursued without it through probability: selecting among several embryos after pre-implantation genetic diagnosis can avoid many single-gene mutations. [00:02:05] Julius says existing screening inequality merely scratches the surface of future polarization, which will extend beyond health. As more people’s DNA is sequenced, he predicts multi-gene patterns will become probabilistically identifiable. He compares this to rapid progress in large language models such as OpenAI’s GPT-4 and ChatGPT, saying their pattern recognition extends beyond language.

[00:02:40] Julius introduces a Stephen Wolfram explanation from the Lex Fridman podcast about language models and patterns humans struggle to recognize. In the clip, Wolfram says Aristotle stopped too quickly: more formal structures, or small “algebras,” can be extracted from language. Going from A to B and B to C means going from A to C, whereas A being B’s friend and B being C’s friend does not mean A is C’s friend. The route’s transitivity holds regardless of whether one flies, walks or swims.

### G003 [00:03:48–00:05:26]

[00:03:48] Wolfram continues that aspects of language capture features of how the world works. He says ChatGPT effectively discovered logic as Aristotle did—by noticing patterns in many sentences—but seems to be discovering something more complicated, a “semantic grammar.” The podcast exchange calls this the “laws of language” or “laws of thought”; Wolfram says the latter was George Boole’s title for his Boolean algebra in 1830.

[00:04:40] Julius argues that language-model pattern recognition transfers to any medium, including genetics: given enough sequenced DNA, models can identify multi-gene patterns humans cannot, including those governing hair color, eye color and probabilistic height, which he says involves tens of thousands of genes. He says the models already exist and the needed data will inevitably accumulate. ### G004 [00:05:28–00:07:07]

[00:05:28] Julius refers to risks involving “[unclear] biology” and reiterates that, despite the genome’s complexity, sufficient data will make multi-gene patterns probabilistically identifiable. He says roughly 30 million genomes have been sequenced among over eight billion living people. [00:06:08] He agrees that selecting among only five or six embryos would not offer drastically unusual options, but imagines a million, with their data displayed and filterable on a dashboard like an avatar creator. ### G005 [00:07:09–00:08:59]

[00:07:09] Julius qualifies that environment influences IQ and personality, but says genes play a massive role and both physical and mental genetic traits greatly affect one’s future. He reiterates that sufficiently data-rich models will soon identify their complex multi-gene patterns.

[00:07:30] The account explains a proposed route to choosing from millions: after years of research, Shinya Yamanaka and his team identified four “master genes,” or Yamanaka factors, that can turn adult cells back into induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs), equivalent to embryonic stem cells. Just as stem cells can differentiate into skin, blood, liver, heart and other human cell types, the factors can reverse that developmental clock. The account says Yamanaka and Gurdon won the 2012 Nobel Prize for discoveries potentially revolutionizing biology, including egg production; it also says stem cells made from skin cells mean embryos need not necessarily be sacrificed for research, and reiterates Yamanaka’s 2012 physiology or medicine prize.

[00:08:42] The account says Japanese cell biologists Katsuhiko Hayashi and Mitinori Saito announced in 2012 that they had used Yamanaka factors to reprogram adult mouse skin cells into iPS cells, then added chemicals to produce egg and sperm precursor cells.

### G006 [00:09:02–00:10:46]

[00:09:02] The account continues that the artificial precursors matured into eggs in mouse ovaries and sperm in mouse testes; mouse IVF using them produced what it calls perfectly healthy baby mice.

[00:09:21] It contrasts the approximately 15 eggs obtained in an average woman’s extraction with the potential scale of induced stem-cell technology. In an illustrative scenario, 100 milliliters of blood taken by an assistant contains around 100 million peripheral blood mononuclear cells, or PBMCs—blood cells with nuclei. [00:10:16] The proposed process would yield thousands rather than roughly 15 fertilized eggs. Advanced AI tools could sort them for optimal shape and biology, a technological version of embryologists’ manual work. The eggs would then grow for five to seven days into roughly 100-cell blastocysts, from each of which about five cells would be extracted and sequenced. The narration concludes that this explains the technology for choosing, with the sentence continuing beyond the excerpt.

### G007 [00:10:49–00:12:36]

[00:10:49] Julius predicts that wealthy people who can afford to produce genetically ideal offspring will raise “high IQ tall Chads” and beautiful, smart “stacies,” endowed with ideal environments and genetics in every aspect. Addressing his many “black pilled” viewers, he says “it’s not over,” perhaps “it never began,” but they can begin now by using time productively, making more money, and striving for an ideal future for themselves and potentially their offspring.

[00:12:18] Julius calls himself about as black-pilled as possible, meaning he strictly believes in the selfish-gene principle and evolution. # Defending Gerbert Johnson Against Einstein | Free Listening Comprehension Transgression Guide

- Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=4gcCkGUMSWA
- Published (UTC): 2023-07-31T01:40:16+00:00
- Source: consolidated from timestamped transcript; NOT independently fact-checked

### G001 [00:00:01–00:02:27]

[00:00:01] An opening with music and fragmentary, partly unintelligible speech invokes a fight to expose the truth, people lost in the process, a new generation, and remaining together.

[00:00:56] Julius says Gerbert Johnson’s video “Why Young Men Aren’t Growing Up” was attacked by YouTuber Vaush, who was not open-minded and had already decided to discredit Gerbert. Brief inserted fragments include a reference to “statutory,” a partly unintelligible account of fleeing and climbing a tree, and a reaction that someone skipped half the video and might not go back; “late bloomer” is also mentioned. A comic exchange disputes whether Kevin Bacon was in *Footloose*, ending “you lose.”

[00:01:43] Julius contrasts considering Gerbert’s arguments with dismissing them. An inserted speaker predicts, from the video’s opening frames, that the problems will be dismissed with “go outside”; a viewer comment says the video captures thoughts they have daily and shows many people are in the same situation. The speaker agrees going outside is good advice but says it does not address why the advice must be given, and is not a censored “revolutionary idea” nobody has thought of.

### G002 [00:02:29–00:04:29]

[00:02:29] The preceding speaker hopes actual problems will be acknowledged. Julius sarcastically calls “just go outside bro” an insightful suggestion and accuses Vaush of scoring semantic points instead of considering Gerbert’s message, calling this prejudice. He says people like Vaush prioritize virtue-signaling inclusiveness and moral superiority.

[00:03:07] An inserted clip, partly unclear at its start, mentions zoophile material and says it should be legal; the speaker calls it a hot take that they have not heard a convincing moral or legal argument for making possession of child pornography illegal. Another fragment says “actual child.” Julius proposes replacing “incel” with another derogatory phrase for being something involuntarily, then generalizing about and dismissing anything potentially involving those people; a brief inserted remark calls “these books” pathetic. He sarcastically asks whether these are “just semantics.”

[00:03:44] Julius asks how Vaush can be narrow-minded on some subjects and open-minded on others; another inserted fragment is partly unintelligible and mentions “owning a child.” Julius suggests audience feedback may explain the contrast: older contrarian notions were unpopular, while mocking incels is newly fashionable and supposedly virtuous—“just ask Assad.” He praises Gerbert’s video for addressing valid concerns society, like Vaush, dismisses, beginning with rising escapism.

### G003 [00:04:32–00:06:16]

[00:04:32] Julius lists Gerbert’s concerns: declining community, college affordability, and atomized people lacking purpose beyond consumption and escapism. He says this generation, especially men, shows widespread stunted development, citing men leaving the labor force, college entry at 60% women and 40% men, and graduation at an even more skewed 70–30. Some say men avoid or leave college to pursue ambitions such as business; Julius allows this may be true for some and probably was the idea for most, but says many are simply “[censored] up.”

[00:05:19] He also cites Gen Z’s obsession with escapism and fantasy: liking them is fine, but he finds it striking how many make them nearly their whole personality. He connects this to dying community and says Gerbert used fantasy and games as examples; although the intended message was clear, Vaush seized on convention images to score points.

[00:05:52] In an inserted response, Gerbert acknowledges realizing after upload that the convention pictures actually showed community and people having fun, contrary to his intended portrayal. He says a better image would have been a solitary “hikikomori weeaboo” in a room covered in posters. The discussion then turns to the estimate that people indulge in escapism alone more often.

### G004 [00:06:18–00:07:58]

[00:06:18] The speaker argues that people indulge in escapism alone far more often than they attend conventions, and some never attend. Conventions are fun, involve photographs, and may require travel, but are occasional events rather than dependable, frequent social settings for building lasting relationships; people can meet there, as at other events, but the speaker would not call that a community.

[00:06:59] Julius reiterates that Vaush seeks semantic points and tries to discredit Gerbert at every opportunity, though most viewers—and perhaps Vaush—understood his meaning. In the featured exchange, Gerbert says community and culture are dying; Vaush responds that the examples are community Gerbert dislikes, and culture is not dying but is as rich as or richer than ever, with contributions from more varied people. How people engage with it has changed, and it may be unhealthy, but “dying” feeds alarmist narratives. A responding speaker concedes “dying” may be the wrong term and suggests “degrading,” or changing for the worse.

### G005 [00:07:59–00:09:41]

[00:07:59] Julius says Gerbert calls fantasy obsessions childish, while Vaush argues obsession with fantasy is not necessarily consumerism or childishness: it can indicate creativity. Vaush cites J.R.R. Tolkien, who channeled his obsession into a bedrock of Western literary and fantasy culture.

[00:08:42] Julius calls Tolkien an outlier and the example cherry-picking, asserting that most people indulge for escapism—for example, turning on a console after work, going to bed, and repeating. Vaush advises balancing it with a fulfilling life.

[00:09:01] Gerbert acknowledges the point that creators’ obsessions produce great art, including video games, and names Shakespeare, Tolkien, George R.R. Martin, game designers and, uncertainly, Todd Howard. He nevertheless calls Vaush’s objection a stingy attack on his wording: he does not mean those creators are childish or that being interested in something is cringe, but is concerned about young men constantly immersed in consuming games, anime and similar escapism.

### G006 [00:09:43–00:11:22]

[00:09:43] Gerbert continues that many such men seem to have little else and lack the balance Vaush describes, living for escapism. Julius says this imbalance is precisely the video’s point and why many men are not growing up, then sarcastically apologizes for forgetting Vaush’s “brilliant solution”: “just go outside.”

[00:10:20] A clip has Gerbert say some men were smart and had potential, but “it’s over now.” Vaush objects that it is not over for a 20-year-old who likes fantasy, telling him to shut up and calling the remark whiny, mindless “Doomer aestheticism” that manipulates emotions with a fake sense of finality. Gerbert responds that Vaush is misconstruing him: he is not a doomer, the video ends positively, and he doubts Vaush will reach the end. He begins clarifying that he is not saying these men’s lives are over because they enjoyed something, with the sentence continuing beyond the excerpt.

### G007 [00:11:24–00:13:03]

- [00:12:17] Julius says Gerbert is not a doomer and did not mean his audience’s lives were over when he said “it’s over”; he accuses Vaush of virtue-signaling by exploiting the phrase, although Julius thinks Vaush understood the implication.
- [00:12:40] In a clip, Gerbert compares himself with his father at 20, saying his father had lived more and experienced more growth and character development. Vaush objects that people in earlier generations did not necessarily have rich, varied, exciting lives: historically, many spent their lives on one farm and died early.

### G008 [00:13:05–00:14:51]

- [00:13:05] Vaush says earlier generations may have suffered more and grown up faster because life was harder and allowed less fun, but life is not a race to prioritize financial and personal responsibilities over enjoyment. He asks whether the supposed growth of an 11-year-old who escapes an abusive father and performs oral sex to survive on the streets would be enviable.
- [00:13:51] Julius says Vaush also disputes Gerbert’s wish to live decades ago, before current atomization and technology. Julius thinks both sides merit discussion because happiness is relative to one’s experience, but says Vaush lectures that Gerbert is wrong in every respect and cites a bizarre example.
- [00:14:20] Gerbert agrees that many past lives were monotonous and some “character development” was suffering he should not envy. He counters that Zoomers spend enormous amounts of time on social media, games, YouTube and screens, which he initially calls no experience at all.

### G009 [00:14:54–00:16:29]

He says the quality of past experience was almost irrelevant to him: despite acknowledging the street-child example sounds bad, he, as a Zoomer with limited experience, envies and idealizes people who lived without the internet and were “actually living” all the time.
- [00:15:55] Julius says Gerbert’s video blowing up shows his observation resonates with many people. Going outside and meeting people is possible, but Julius says that response misses the video’s point; he reiterates that Gerbert is not a doomer.
- [00:16:21] Gerbert says he had not considered how isolating leaving high school without going to university would be. Vaush begins responding that school is when people are forced to socialize.

### G010 [00:16:32–00:18:03]

- [00:16:32] Vaush says school is the only period when the systems around people incentivize making friends and getting along, but losing that support does not make friendship impossible. He says people 200 years ago generally had no schooling yet met through acquaintances or in town, and people can still go out, attend events and engage with others.
- [00:17:08] Gerbert agrees that people can make the effort, but says there are problems: when he goes outside, people are elderly, while peers are often in college, where he is an outsider. He frequently meets people and may see them once or twice, but usually finds nothing sustainable without an established community.

Julius then says he completely agrees with things Vaush says next and believes Gerbert shares that mentality, leaving him confused about why Vaush calls the video pathetic; not everyone making contrarian observations is a doomer.
- [00:18:36] Vaush says life is harder than it should be but friendship remains possible with work. He rejects excuses from friendless chatters, including anxiety and shyness: people’s desired levels of social contact differ, but everyone needs someone, and in-person friends are valuable. He urges effort and calls fearful viewers cowards.
- [00:19:13] Gerbert calls this a “based rant,” agreeing that people coping by citing anxiety should stop making excuses and put in effort. Julius says Vaush’s handling of comments reveals a narrow perspective many share: a commenter says the video expressed daily thoughts and showed others were in the same situation; Vaush responds, “go outside.” Julius introduces Gerbert’s response as a good summary.

### G012 [00:19:48–00:21:30]

# Just Shut Up

- Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=e-Z99gV6esg
- Published (UTC): 2023-08-20T14:08:08+00:00
- Source: consolidated from timestamped transcript; NOT independently fact-checked

### G001 [00:00:00–00:01:55]

[00:00:00] Julius recounts that Nicholas I ascended the Russian throne in 1825 amid a liberal rebellion demanding modernization. After crushing it, he sentenced a leader, whose name is transcribed uncertainly as “realev,” to death. At the hanging, the rope broke; Julius says such apparent miracles were then typically grounds for pardon. Bruised on the ground, the man remarked that Russians could do nothing properly, not even make rope.

[00:00:54] A messenger told Nicholas, who was disappointed but began signing a pardon. Asked what the prisoner had said, the messenger repeated the rope remark; Nicholas replied, “Well then let us prove the contrary.” Julius says the man was hanged again the next day, jokes that the rope broke again, then says he died. He calls him a “[censored] idiot,” though possibly he was not one, and says that is nonetheless how he is remembered.

[00:01:43] Julius imagines that, had the man instead merely lost his job and been canceled, among other consequences, he would convince himself the remark had been worth it for his principles and ideals; the thought continues into the next group.

### G002 [00:01:58–00:03:42]

[00:01:58] Julius calls that imagined justification delusion and the same “cope” listeners use after saying things they probably should not. He argues that the temporary satisfaction can cost someone a job and impair their quality of life: they may imagine being seen as a fearless outlier who stands by their principles and ignores others’ opinions, but people will forget them in two weeks while the consequences may last much longer.

[00:02:43] He recommends weighing risks, rewards, pros and cons because words cannot be taken back. As an example of the current climate, he says someone can be ridiculed online and lose a job over comments about a bodega shop. A brief inserted voice says, “Ladies and gentlemen, I’m here today to apologize,” followed by “Why did you say—” before Julius resumes.

[00:03:13] With statements able to go viral in a few phone clicks, he says practicing restraint of the tongue matters more than ever. He expects most viewers to disagree, says he understands their argument and grants that quality of life is a matter of perspective, but calls their perspective flawed, misinformed and clouded by emotion.

### G003 [00:03:44–00:05:42]

[00:03:44] Julius says listeners repeatedly get the worse end of a trade-off because emotion makes them unable to resist temporary satisfaction. Usually, he says, this is not about cancellation but about saying something unfavorable to friends or family and becoming less likable.

[00:04:07] An inserted exchange includes “Not famous,” “You’re in trouble,” “Why?”, a censored remark mentioning crypto, someone calling to Steve to “get his ass and run out,” greetings, and a claim about having just done a “raw” and “real” podcast with Tana Mojo.

[00:04:38] Julius says a person left without friends may console themselves that they are merely honest and that Steve Jobs was honest and successful. He instead characterizes them as addicted to saying stupid things for temporary satisfaction, or as trying to show how smart they are.

[00:04:57] He claims people with above-average IQ recognize patterns, contradictions and double standards well, and frequently point them out in politics and controversial discussions of race, sexuality, gender or policy. He says these contradictions exist on both ends of the spectrum, and such people seize every opportunity to discuss them to demonstrate their intelligence, at least in their own view.

### G004 [00:05:45–00:08:15]

[00:05:45] Julius contrasts IQ with practical intelligence: regardless of IQ or whether they recognize contradictions, he claims people with very high practical intelligence avoid these discussions or pretend to agree because it serves their quality of life. Many high-IQ people, he says, fail to understand that bringing up facts will only alienate the other party.

[00:06:37] He claims media exploit this by publishing stories containing contradictions or double standards that people feel compelled to quote, retweet and comment on to show how stupid or unfair they are. In his account, the media want people to notice, feel that way and think themselves smart; the result is greater division, while the commenter is just another cog in the world.

[00:07:24] Music follows, with a brief “thank you.” [00:08:02] Julius offers an exception: controversial statements may be worthwhile if one can monetize or otherwise benefit from them, or has a larger plan for an audience being built from them. He adds, “Feel free to subscribe, by the way.”

### G005 [00:08:17–00:09:20]

[00:08:17] Reiterating his pros-and-cons framework, Julius says more power to anyone who makes the benefits of controversial statements outweigh the costs. He believes the overwhelming majority of viewers have no such plan, especially in conversation with friends, and are instead acting emotionally and unable to tame their tongues.

[00:08:43] He recommends that viewers who spot a contradiction among friends notice the burning desire to call it out, restrain themselves and see how long they can refrain. He concludes, “Just shut up—it’ll pay dividends,” followed by music.

# Just Pretend To Be Normal

- Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=WdwwFVNsmLM
- Published (UTC): 2023-09-11T00:02:19+00:00
- Source: consolidated from timestamped transcript; NOT independently fact-checked

### G001 [00:00:00–00:02:01]

[00:00:00] Julius describes late-1500s Italy as violent amid the Protestant Reformation’s challenge to the Catholic Church and authority. He says many suffered, including Galileo, but philosopher Tommaso Campanella suffered even more. Campanella disbelieved in miracles, heaven and hell, believing instead that the Church promoted such superstitions to control ordinary people through fear.

[00:00:30] Julius says Campanella carelessly shared these atheistic, contrarian beliefs publicly and was imprisoned by the Inquisition in 1593. Six years later he was partially released to a Naples monastery, where he joined a plan to overthrow Spanish invaders in southern Italy. The Italian Inquisition and its counterparts imprisoned him again and tortured him to understand his beliefs. Julius describes one method, transcribed as “La Vega” or “La Villa,” as slowly suspending victims onto sharp spikes that pierced their skin at the slightest contact.

[00:01:18] Julius says Campanella learned about power and changed his strategy, not his beliefs: he disguised their outward appearance and pleaded insanity to save his life, presenting the ideas as coming from an uncontrollable part of his mind. Torture continued for a while, but his sentence was eventually changed to life imprisonment. Chained to a dungeon wall for the first four years, he nevertheless continued writing.

### G002 [00:02:03–00:03:58]

[00:02:03] Julius says Campanella became more strategic, sharing ideas indirectly. His book *The Hispanic Monarchy* claimed Spain had a divine mission to expand worldwide—the opposite of his own views—as a bold show of conversion to orthodoxy. Julius says it worked and he was freed six years later.

[00:02:36] After his release, Campanella wrote *Atheism Conquered*, ostensibly attacking freethinkers in debates where Catholicism supposedly defeated heresy. Julius says readers found that its heretical arguments, never previously expressed outside the book, were bold and convincing, while the Catholic arguments were clichéd, convoluted, tiresome and unconvincing—though they were arguments Catholics themselves used. Nobody could really claim he deserved imprisonment again. Julius calls this “4D chess”: by pretending to disagree with his own opinions, Campanella published them indirectly.

### G003 [00:04:01–00:05:50]

[00:04:01] Julius continues that Campanella gave his opinions exposure without being tortured again: receptive people understood his intentions while others looked away. The book became popular among those who agreed with him, serving as a sort of Bible.

[00:04:22] Julius says people will always rebel against oppression with ideas perhaps ahead of their time, but displaying contrarian beliefs is pointless if it only brings suffering and persecution. He says martyrdom serves no purpose; it is better to live, even thrive, in an oppressive world. He recommends delivering ideas strategically and delicately to those who may understand, without changing one’s beliefs.

[00:04:59] Julius claims people learn young to lie and disguise feelings, and complete honest expression is socially impossible. For most this comes naturally, he says, pointing to the comments on any girl’s Instagram post. Others regard it as an unbearable infringement on freedom and insist on sharing contrarian beliefs and superior values, yet convince few and offend many. Clever people, he says, can behave normally and speak conventionally without thinking that way. He introduces Sam Bankman-Fried as an example, claiming he never believed the “woke” ideology he preached.

### G004 [00:05:52–00:07:29]

[00:05:52] Julius says Bankman-Fried understood that FTX needed media and public support to thrive despite the fraud. He claims most large companies preach the same beliefs, while executives privately “don’t give a [word omitted]” and care instead about ESG scores, media support and the bottom line, not airing their own opinions.

[00:06:21] Julius says nobody likes the brutally honest friend who constantly disputes a group’s consensus. The truly smartest person, he claims, is the friend who silently agrees with someone’s complex opinions but says nothing to avoid making enemies. He predicts life will improve if people pretend to think normally, recommending mainstream TV and music so they can converse with ordinary people.

[00:07:00] Julius tells viewers they are complex thinkers drawn to his videos and says some previously covered topics are very contrarian and should never be discussed publicly because doing so will not gain friends. He reiterates that they may keep thinking that way but should pretend to act normal, again guaranteeing a better quality of life. If they must express their opinions, he says, they should do so only with their closest friends.

### G005 [00:07:31–00:08:26]

[00:07:31] Even with close friends, Julius recommends being strategic like Campanella, perhaps presenting an opinion as something one is arguing against or merely considering.

[00:07:42] Beyond daily life, Julius advises aspiring powerful people to withhold contrarian notions until they have gained power. He says elected officials do this, implementing ideas only after election; people are consequently surprised when officials do things they had ruled out or never discussed, since otherwise they would not have been elected.

[00:08:13] Julius quotes and attributes to Machiavelli: “For a long time I have not said what I believed, nor do I believe what I say, and if indeed I do tell the truth, I hide it among so many lies that it’s hard to find.”

### G003 [00:03:58–00:05:47]

[00:03:58] Julius says Campanella’s intended audience understood his views while others looked away; the popular book became a kind of Bible for those who agreed with him. Julius argues that society always has people who rebel against oppression with ideas perhaps ahead of their time, but displaying contrarian views is pointless if it brings suffering and persecution. He says martyrdom serves no purpose: it is better to survive and thrive, delivering ideas strategically and delicately to those who might understand, without changing one’s beliefs.

[00:05:00] Julius says people learn young to lie and conceal their feelings, and complete truthful expression is socially impossible. He claims this comes naturally to most, citing the comments on any girl’s Instagram post, regardless of who she is. Others find concealment unbearable and an infringement on freedom, insisting on sharing contrarian beliefs and superior value; he says they convince few and offend many. Clever people, he says, can behave normally and speak conventionally without thinking that way. He introduces Sam Bankman-Fried as an example.

### G004 [00:05:49–00:07:24]

[00:05:49] Julius claims Bankman-Fried did not believe the “woke ideology” he preached, but needed media and public support for FTX to thrive despite fraud. Julius similarly claims most large companies preach those beliefs while executives privately do not care, focusing instead on ESG scores, media support and the bottom line, rather than publicizing their own opinions.

[00:06:20] In daily life, Julius says, nobody likes a brutally honest friend who constantly challenges group consensus. He tells viewers that the truly smartest person may be the friend who silently agrees with their complex opinions but says nothing to avoid making enemies. He recommends pretending to think normally and consuming mainstream television and music to converse with normal people, while retaining one’s actual thoughts.

[00:07:00] Julius says many viewers are complex thinkers drawn to his videos, including past contrarian topics. He recommends never discussing those topics publicly because it will not gain friends, and reiterates that acting normal will greatly improve their quality of life.

### G005 [00:07:27–00:08:27]

[00:07:27] Julius recommends that anyone who must express such opinions do so only with their closest friends and, like Campanella, strategically—perhaps presenting the ideas as something they are arguing against or considering.

[00:07:43] For those seeking power, Julius recommends withholding contrarian ideas until they have attained it. He claims elected officials often do this, executing undisclosed or contradicted positions after election because otherwise they would never have been elected, surprising voters.

[00:08:14] He closes with a quotation: “For a long time I have not said what I believed, nor do I believe what I say, and if indeed I do tell the truth, I hide it among so many lies that it’s hard to find,” followed by an attribution transcribed as “Maki.”

# How To Win Any Argument

- Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=MfNm43IYKOk
- Published (UTC): 2023-09-15T23:42:32+00:00
- Source: consolidated from timestamped transcript; NOT independently fact-checked

### G001 [00:00:00–00:02:01]

[00:00:00] Julius recounts that in 131 BC the Roman consul Publius Musianus needed a battering ram to breach the walls of the Greek town of Pergaments. Having seen large rams in an Athens shipyard days earlier, he ordered the largest.

[00:00:17] The engineer argued at length with the soldiers, using diagrams to show that a smaller mast would gain more speed, generate more force and be easier to transport. He said he was the expert and they did not know what they were talking about; Julius says he was indeed Athens’s finest engineer. Knowing their master, the soldiers told him to swallow his expertise and obey.

[00:01:03] After they left, the engineer decided the larger mast would fail and sent the smaller one, expecting Musianus to recognize its superiority and reward him. On its arrival, the confused consul heard from the soldiers that the engineer had argued for the smaller mast but eventually agreed to send the larger. Furious, Musianus summoned him; the engineer gladly repeated his arguments with facts and diagrams.

### G002 [00:02:03–00:04:04]

[00:02:03] The engineer added that it was important in those times to listen to experts and that the consul would not regret it. Musianus let him finish, then had him stripped naked, flogged and “scored with rods”; he died.

[00:02:36] Julius contrasts this with an account of Michelangelo in 1502: he undertook to turn a valuable, previously damaged stone into a sculpture of David holding a sling. After weeks of work, as he was applying the finishing touches, Florence’s mayor, Piero Soderini, visited and admired it but thought the nose too big.

[00:03:11] Michelangelo realized Soderini’s viewing angle made the nose appear larger. Without arguing, he motioned for him to follow up the scaffolding, taking a chisel and marble dust. With Soderini below him, he tapped the nose and let the dust fall, pretending to alter it without actually doing so. From his new vantage point, Soderini said, “I like it better, you’ve made it come alive.”

### G003 [00:04:07–00:05:40]

[00:04:07] Julius says Michelangelo knew arguing with Soderini, a patron who fancied himself a connoisseur, would gain nothing and risk future commissions; changing the nose could ruin his work and the valuable marble. Instead, he brought Soderini closer, correcting his perspective without revealing why the nose had appeared too big. Julius presents this as winning through actions rather than words.

[00:04:43] Julius argues that one cannot know words’ long-term effects: someone may politely concede while inwardly growing resentful. In heated debates people use unverifiable statistics, religious anecdotes and personal experience, which he says do not matter or make them look smart. He claims Ben Shapiro and Steven Crowder’s debate videos are entertainment, not genuine persuasion; at best, opponents concede politely. He recommends not behaving like them in public, saying nobody likes that person’s presence.

[00:05:35] He suggests viewers probably have complex, contrarian opinions because they watch his channel.

### G004 [00:05:42–00:07:04]

[00:05:42] Julius says such opinions are fine but recommends against trying to convince people of them. In rare cases where one must argue, he reiterates that one should do so through actions, claiming words never actually convince anybody.

[00:05:59] As an example, he says some viewers may hold black-pill beliefs supported by data, statistics and personal experience. But showing dating-app statistics or recounting experience to someone unwilling to believe will not persuade them: at best, they will agree politely while coming to resent the speaker. Referring to his previous two videos, he again discourages this and recommends generally not sharing many contrarian opinions, while acknowledging that arguments may sometimes be necessary.

[00:06:43] He reiterates winning through actions: if friends call someone frugal, rather than listing times they paid for food, they could offer the first round of drinks. If a girlfriend calls someone boring, rather than recounting unique things done for her, he proposes another demonstration.

### G005 [00:07:06–00:08:05]

[00:07:06] Julius completes the girlfriend example: scroll through a photo album of places they have traveled together while she sits nearby. If a boss denies a raise after a massive deal, he recommends leaving the deal documents on the desk alongside an open LinkedIn job-search tab rather than mentioning the deal. For a bank teller saying there is no account balance, he says to “pull out your”—the thought cuts off without an intelligible completion.

[00:07:33] He concludes that demonstrating an idea through actions makes the other party less defensive and more open to persuasion: “The truth is generally seen, rarely heard.” Music follows.

# How To Actually Get What You Want

- Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=yjXVDCs7UZE
- Published (UTC): 2023-09-21T01:57:59+00:00
- Source: consolidated from timestamped transcript; NOT independently fact-checked

### G001 [00:00:04–00:02:07]

[00:00:04] Julius recounts that in early-1300s Lucca, Italy, the powerful Paggio family helped Castruccio Castracani rise from soldier to lord. Feeling forgotten once he was powerful, they plotted to dethrone him while he fought Florence; riots and tensions arose between their supporters.

[00:00:39] Stefano, the family’s oldest member, persuaded both sides to lay down their weapons, arguing that fighting would be a fruitless bloodbath and that he should privately persuade Castracani to meet their demands. Castracani returned immediately on hearing the news. Stefano visited, expecting gratitude for restoring peace; he cited that achievement and the family’s role in Castracani’s rise, saying fairness required a pardon and a hearing for their demands. Castracani listened without apparent anger or resentment, said justice would prevail, and invited the whole family to the palace to discuss the demands more efficiently.

### G002 [00:02:09–00:04:25]

[00:02:09] Julius says the entire Paggio family arrived days later and was imprisoned and executed, including Stefano. He calls Stefano a failure for invoking past favors and appealing to Castracani’s mercy and gratitude.

[00:02:44] Julius contrasts Genghis Khan’s trusted adviser Yelü Chucai. He says that by the 12th century Chinese culture had thrived for over 2,000 years, but Khan intended to exterminate the Chinese, level their cities and let grass grow. Chucai, a foreigner who appreciated Chinese culture, persuaded him he could instead gain riches by taxing the inhabitants.

[00:03:39] Julius says that during the conquest of Kaifeng, Khan intended to massacre its inhabitants, as he regularly did to resisting cities. Chucai persuaded him to spare them because the finest engineers had fled there and could be put to use. Khan agreed again, and Chucai got what he wanted. Julius says Khan had never shown such mercy before, but Chucai knew it was not about mercy: he regarded Khan as a barbarian interested in warfare and practical results, not culture.

### G003 [00:04:27–00:06:01]

[00:04:27] Julius says Chucai appealed to the one emotion that would work on Khan: greed. He argues that self-interest moves people: rather than remind them of past help, as Stefano did, offer something they stand to gain, as Chucai did.

[00:04:57] For someone facing dismissal, Julius recommends emphasizing the complexity of an ongoing project and how it would collapse without them, rather than years of service and sacrifice. He asks viewers to subscribe for a future video on becoming irreplaceable.

[00:05:19] He says begging for mercy generally is not ideal. If a girlfriend is breaking up with someone, he recommends offering her value instead of begging for another chance: getting lean and attractive again if one has let oneself go, or making more money if it is a financially based “beta bucks” relationship. He says he is not recommending the latter arrangement, but “to each their own,” and that he is trying to be objective.

[00:05:54] He asks why elderly people are often grateful for conversation and answers that hardly anyone goes out of their way to talk to them.

### G004 [00:06:02–00:07:43]

[00:06:02] Julius attributes people’s neglect of elderly people to their having nothing to offer others’ self-interest. He asks those angry at society’s cruelty and unfairness because they struggle to make friends or get girls when they last went out of their way to converse with an elderly person.

[00:06:23] He reiterates that getting what one wants requires appealing to someone’s self-interest, which varies by person and request. He identifies a reversal: some gain from exercising generosity, mercy or charity, whether through publicity, emotion, self-image, feeling powerful or displaying a good heart. Thus begging can benefit them, as in giving a homeless person a dollar to feel good.

[00:07:05] Julius says “simping” can therefore rarely be effective: a person might find a better partner but lose the constant emotional validation and power they have over the supplicant’s “business.” How much they value that depends on personality. He says this still subtly offers something they want, though most people do not want or prioritize it.

### G005 [00:07:45–00:08:13]

[00:07:45] Julius reiterates that one must offer something appealing to the target’s self-interest, adapting to each target and request and perhaps studying them.

[00:07:55] Addressing commenters who say they do go out of their way to talk to elderly people, he calls them rare cases who are displaying their virtue by saying so. He asks them not to delete their comments, calling them an interesting exhibit for other viewers.

# Are Ugly People More Dangerous? - Lookism & Subconscious Bias

- Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=IaY9zK191RA

[00:00:01] Julius describes Muhammad and Johnny committing the same armed robbery with the same kind of pistol in the same year, but Muhammad receiving a significantly harsher sentence; psychologists later rated Johnny substantially more attractive on average. Anticipating the objection that this is another video proving “pretty privilege,” he says he instead wants to ask whether it benefits society. He voices the reaction that the question itself is repulsive; music follows.

[00:00:54] Julius says a harsher sentence based on appearance is plainly wrong at the individual level, but asks about utilitarianism, which he defines as judging actions right if they benefit a majority. For such sentencing to benefit society, less attractive people would, on average, have to pose a greater risk than more attractive people. Before considering that “deranged” possibility, he says judges and jurors do not consciously weigh attractiveness: Rod Hollier’s article *Physical Attractiveness Bias in the Legal System* suggests the factor is subconscious. Whether or not one accepts Hollier’s conclusions from the studies cited, Julius thinks that, if the bias exists, it is more likely subconscious, as Malcolm Gladwell discusses in *Blink*.

### G002 [00:02:09–00:03:51]

[00:02:09] Continuing the reference to Gladwell, Julius says subconscious influences occur more often than people would like to believe. He asks whether human brains evolved to think this way, claiming that genetic makeup heavily influences actions and that those actions were positively selected in evolution.

[00:02:30] An illustrative passage argues that infidelity was positively selected and connects concealed ovulation to women having affairs with men of supposedly superior genetics, then deceiving their partners into raising the offspring. It calls this horrible but says evolution is not guided by fairness or justice: genes replicate at whatever cost, making infidelity a biological “feature,” not a bug. The attribution of the passage is not explicit in the transcript.

[00:03:17] Julius asks whether jurors’ supposed subconscious tendency to see attractive people as less dangerous was passed down for thousands of years by chance or has an evolutionary reason. He stresses that he is not saying the bias is right; he is questioning biology and does not have the answer.

### G003 [00:03:54–00:05:46]

[00:03:54] Julius asks why no one has questioned the behavior’s existence, saying it occurs in the legal system, social situations and even parking lots. A passage states that attractive people are perceived as more intelligent—“what is beautiful is good”—and that this is not necessarily romantic: neither the judge’s nor the judged person’s sex changes the perception, and studies reportedly show first- and second-graders consider attractive teachers more intelligent.

[00:04:35] Julius proposes an explanation for involuntary bias, even in supposedly impartial jurors. He claims 50% more women than men successfully passed on their DNA, so people have 50% more female ancestors; one man sleeping with multiple women illustrates how many other men reproduce with no women and are removed from the gene pool.

[00:05:04] A separate-sounding explanatory passage describes individuals as replicators whose effects are called phenotypes: replicators producing the best “machines,” or fit phenotypes, increase in number, while those that fail replicate less and eventually become extinct. The speaker is not identified in the transcript.

### G004 [00:05:48–00:07:31]

[00:05:48] The preceding explanation concludes that unsuccessful replicators eventually go extinct. Julius then contrasts human concealed ovulation with chimpanzees, saying it means the female chooses rather than males fighting over her. A separate-sounding passage says female sexual selection was a major force differentiating humans from chimps: chimp females in estrus mate indiscriminately, and dominant males leave more offspring by chasing away subordinates, not through female choice. It claims human concealed ovulation and intense female selection of men mean people have **twice** as many female as male ancestors, differing from the earlier 50% figure.

[00:06:31] Julius alludes to a horrific crime committed when a man is not selected but wants a woman anyway, asking listeners to imagine how much more often it happened before cameras and thousands of years ago. He proposes that women who feared such men survived and passed on their genes more often, giving male offspring the same tendencies. He reiterates that the sex of neither the judge nor the judged affects the perception, calling this natural selection.

[00:07:10] He suggests women’s reluctance to be bluntly honest to unattractive men reflects not only kindness but subconscious fear of violence. A separate-sounding passage adds that rejection makes a man acutely self-conscious because the woman, as “mother nature,” is effectively saying he may be acceptable as a friend but his genetic material should not propagate.

### G005 [00:07:34–00:09:19]

[00:07:43] Julius says existence’s entire purpose is reproduction and invokes Richard Dawkins’s description of people as survival machines for replicating genes. A passage attributed to Dawkins explains that the difference between successful and unsuccessful genes matters over millions of years: successful genes build bodies and control embryological processes that preserve and pass them on; the individual body is a “survival machine.”

[00:08:31] Julius claims everything people do and feel follows from the desire to reproduce. Hypothetically, realizing one is unlikely to reproduce and thus has failed life’s purpose could have horrific consequences; sometimes people with nothing to lose are the most dangerous. He mentions his video *Is Your Rejection Paving the Way for a Better Future?* and says failure to fulfill this purpose could have drastic implications. He declines to spell out examples, expecting viewers to infer them from correlations with certain events, and says acknowledging this upsets him.

### G006 [00:09:21–00:11:14]

[00:09:21] Julius says most people are not like the dangerous outliers he alludes to, but invokes probability: even one bad apple per tree produces an obvious correlation across thousands of trees. He argues that reducing bad apples means fewer trees, achievable only through natural selective pressure over many years. He says eugenics is never the right answer, claims this selection is already occurring naturally in Western countries, and says other parts of the world appear to be moving in the opposite direction.

[00:10:13] He reiterates his question: is the subconscious assumption that less attractive people are more dangerous coincidence or evolutionary? He says the utilitarian question remains unanswered because it involves more than danger. Apologizing that he researched no studies comparing productivity by attractiveness, he hypothetically assumes less attractive people are more productive on average and asks whether that productivity would outweigh the outliers supposedly more likely to commit crimes or endanger society. He has no idea how to begin answering, and says people can rationalize anything, so there are likely many arguments to consider.

### G007 [00:11:15–00:12:49]

- [00:11:15] Julius asks viewers whether the subconscious behavior is a net benefit to society and invites comments. He says he does not know from a utilitarian perspective: should people trust natural selection and instinct, or are they outdated for modern conditions? Has natural selection had time to adapt to things like cameras?
- [00:11:41] He distinguishes a net societal benefit from whether the behavior is right or wrong, suggesting human lives perhaps should not be considered utilitarianly or measured this way. # The One Way Back - Inception & Physics

- Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=3ZuykQMmAfI
- Published (UTC): 2024-04-04T01:38:14+00:00
- Source: consolidated from timestamped transcript; NOT independently fact-checked

### G001 [00:00:03–00:02:17]

[00:00:03] Music accompanies Julius saying he fears time, not death. Time seems slow while passing, yet its accumulated passage surprises us; waking after either eight hours or 15 minutes can feel as though no time passed. He asks viewers to remember this as he sets out to convince them that returning to the past is possible—not as a play on words, but through physics. They may appreciate the video or call it “deranged”; music follows.

[00:01:08] Julius says romanticizing the past is deeply rooted in psychology, and he intends to explain how to use it to manipulate others and one’s own mind for a happier life. He claims it influences almost all preferences: fans predictably tend to prefer old albums, films or games to new iterations, even with better graphics, plots, acting or quality, because the originals are associated with where they were, whom they played with and how young they were. A new iteration can sometimes win, he says, but must be exponentially better because it competes against both the old work and everything associated with experiencing it.

### G002 [00:02:21–00:04:04]

[00:02:21] Julius explains the preference for the past as wanting what we cannot have: everything we know seems to say we cannot return and re-experience it. Similarly, when a relative, friend or pet dies and cannot return, we appreciate and love them more than during their life, which he calls tragic. He urges spending quality time with parents and friends and telling them they are loved while possible: once they are gone, one would give everything for another chance, and their loss is a matter of when, not if.

[00:03:19] Taking people’s existence for granted does not make someone bad, Julius says; it is human nature. Once someone is definitively gone, one would pay every last dollar to see them again and tends to forget negatives: a pet ruining furniture, someone’s mistreatment or betrayal, or a childhood lack of freedom and authority. He says deliberately recalling the bad is not a good way to cope with what is gone, and introduces another solution.

### G003 [00:04:06–00:05:43]

[00:04:06] Julius proposes “hacking” one’s mind: because some things are not definitively known, he says, they offer opportunities to believe whatever optimizes quality of life. He claims well-known people, including physicists and philosophers, have used variations of this practice. He quotes Einstein as believing in Spinoza’s God, revealed in the orderly harmony of existence rather than concerned with human fates and actions, and as rejecting an afterlife with “one life is enough for me.”

[00:04:55] Julius says that, whether one likes Tate or not, Tate sums up the practice well. In an inserted passage, Tate rejects a paradigm and says he can fix his own problems by changing his reality and creating a satisfying experience of life. He compares two men in separate haunted houses: a nighttime noise leaves the ghost believer paranoid, sleepless and shaking in a corner, while the nonbeliever returns to sleep. He says belief in the ghost, not the ghost itself, punishes the believer. The next claim—“if you do not believe in … you can never be …”—is incomplete or obscured.

### G004 [00:05:47–00:07:43]

[00:05:47] Tate’s inserted passage continues: he does not care if he is wrong because his mental model makes him competitive across human endeavors. If not believing in an idea helps him fight it, feel happier and regulate his emotions, he will remain wrong; he rejects beliefs that take power away in favor of those that make him powerful. Some words identifying the idea are censored or incomplete.

[00:06:18] Julius identifies the key point as Tate acknowledging he might be wrong, rather than arguing science, and choosing beliefs that make him competitive. Likewise, Julius says, truly convincing oneself one can return to childhood memories and tell one’s mother and father “I love you” again would set one free. He asks how a sane, rational, reasonably intelligent person could believe such an apparently irrational idea.

[00:06:58] He introduces “the art of synthesizing theories”: combining multiple physics theories he describes as reasonable, realistic and believable, though not fully proven, can produce bizarre conclusions. He claims that combining determinism, heat death and quantum fluctuations yields one: after the universe reaches maximum entropy, only quantum fluctuations remain, and over infinite time every possibility must eventually occur.

### G005 [00:07:46–00:09:50]

[00:07:46] Julius continues that one eventual quantum fluctuation will reproduce the Big Bang that began this universe’s deterministic cycle. Recalling his comparison of eight hours’ and 15 minutes’ sleep, he says a person will be unconscious during the intervening period and, on going to sleep, wake immediately to relive everything precisely as before because it is deterministic—including watching this video and considering subscribing.

[00:08:22] Acknowledging that this is a lot to take in, he points to his earlier videos on determinism, heat death and quantum fluctuations as ways to convince oneself of reliving the exact same life: childhood, seeing one’s parents, playing with one’s dog and even considering sharing his video with a best friend. He reiterates that being wrong does not matter if the belief improves life. He says he does not think he is insane, nor does he consider insane people who believe an afterlife will reunite them with friends and family; he thinks they know how to live a good life.

[00:09:17] Music plays. Julius closes by asking whether, when the universe restarts, it will really be you or merely a copy of your consciousness.
