# 7 Chess Lessons From Drake vs Kendrick Lamar

- Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=t4OSOc8C0r4
- Published (UTC): 2024-04-21T02:06:37+00:00
- Source: consolidated from timestamped transcript; NOT independently fact-checked

### G001 [00:00:00–00:01:37]

[00:00:00] Julius calls controversies involving Drake and underage girls a devastating potential attack vector for Kendrick Lamar. A brief intervening phrase is unclear.

[00:00:10] He says everyone should pay attention to the feud, regardless of their interest in hip-hop: like politicians’ reputational warfare, its complex strategies and propaganda can affect people subconsciously, manipulate opinion and control the narrative. He proposes lessons applicable to business, competition and social situations.

[00:00:42] Julius argues that Drake recognized this reputational weakness and used a Slim Shady/*8 Mile* approach, putting it on the table before Kendrick could. After responding to Kendrick’s “Like That” verse with “Push Ups,” Drake released a second diss using AI Tupac and Snoop Dogg to speak indirectly about both rappers. Julius says fake Tupac suggests common avenues for attacking Drake, potentially weakening Kendrick’s offense. He suspects the track’s primary motive was not merely to rush Kendrick, but to expose Drake’s own vulnerability first so he could dismiss later attacks.

### G002 [00:01:39–00:03:17]

[00:01:39] Julius completes his point about preempting attacks over the underage-girl controversies; a brief intervening phrase is partially unintelligible.

[00:01:48] He suspects Kendrick baited Drake into doubling down on Michael Jackson comparisons: Drake flipped Kendrick’s “Prince outlived Mike Jack” into “What’s a prince to a king? He’s a son.” Julius says Jackson had controversies involving underage girls and boys, and that Drake realized the trap too late. In his view, the entire “Taylor Made Freestyle” was damage control disguised as an attempt to rush Kendrick; he says it remains to be seen whether Kendrick uses that angle or changes it.

[00:02:26] His first life lesson is not to develop tunnel vision on offense, but to anticipate an opponent’s plans. He says Kendrick used the same preemptive strategy on *Mr. Morale & the Big Steppers*, openly discussing flaws including cheating on his wife and sex addiction, thereby making future attacks harder. Julius reiterates the need to anticipate opponents.

[00:03:03] Lesson two: do not underestimate pawns, which serve important purposes despite amateurs treating them as disposable. Unlike Kendrick, Julius says, Drake has accumulated pawns to protect his reputation, including Adin Ross and DJ Akademiks.

### G003 [00:03:20–00:04:52]

[00:03:20] Julius compares Drake’s allied streamers and influencers to chess pawns: even a devastating attack akin to taking his queen would leave Kendrick facing a crowded board. He says they manipulate the feud’s narrative and shift public opinion without Drake having to speak.

[00:03:47] Commentary, with speaker attribution somewhat unclear, calls Ross and others part of Drake’s “propaganda machine” and says Drake cultivated relationships with Akademiks, Kai and Speed, who influence the internet and young people. An inserted clip features an excited fan greeting Drake and saying he is a huge fan.

[00:04:11] The commentary calls it “genius” to use Ross and Akademiks to spread allegedly false rumors of a pre-prepared Kendrick diss: it portrays Kendrick as obsessed and raises expectations unfairly, making disappointment more likely. An inserted voice demands to hear the supposedly four-year-old “mythical” song meant to rip Drake “limb from limb, hair follicle by hair follicle.”

### G004 [00:04:55–00:06:28]

[00:04:55] The inserted voice finishes calling for “Kung Fu Kenny” to start sending kicks; another remark says the timeline filled with talk of a four-year-old diss kept in the vault.

[00:05:08] Julius reiterates that the conflict extends beyond music: he calls Drake’s use of pawns real, effective wartime propaganda manipulating mass opinion. He says Drake’s sampling of Akademiks at the end of “Push Ups” helps maintain the influential commentator’s bias, almost as if he were indebted.

[00:05:34] Although Kendrick does not appear to use pawns, Julius says Metro Boomin does. He describes Metro as a respected producer who poured gasoline on the beef rather than igniting it, promising to explain later. Unable to send shots himself as a producer, Metro allegedly recruited Future, Kendrick, A$AP Rocky, Rick Ross and the Weeknd to do so while co-signing them on his album. Julius says their possible future need for Metro’s production gives him leverage, just as artists’ possible need for Drake features does; this use of pawns also created a major weakness for Metro’s side.

[00:06:19] Lesson three: appearing to be the underdog can be advantageous in psychological games. Julius introduces Fischer’s victory over Spassky as an example.

### G005 [00:06:31–00:08:04]

[00:06:31] Julius says many people, including the author of *The 48 Laws of Power*, attribute Fischer’s win to his unpredictability and strange behavior. Julius considers it overlooked that Spassky was the favorite and that Fischer deliberately forfeited the second game after losing the first: Spassky supposedly faced immense pressure because the public expected him to win. Julius thinks this pressure significantly contributed to Spassky’s eventual loss.

[00:07:09] He says Drake plays the underdog with “What is this, a 20 v 1?” and a comparison to Black Mamba from *Kill Bill*. Kendrick and the others may not experience Spassky’s live-game pressure, but Julius believes public perception of Drake as the underdog still gives him an advantage.

[00:07:27] Julius recommends appearing to be an underdog to win public support, without necessarily sacrificing confidence. He compares politicians who emphasize that the system is against them even when it is not, and claims Drake wanted this conflict all along but presents himself as its victim because that benefits public opinion. Lesson four follows: always plot and think long term.

### G006 [00:08:06–00:09:38]

[00:08:06] Julius says high-IQ people tend to excel at chess because they calculate combinations many moves ahead, while impatient players do poorly. He considers long-term scheming rare in life and more common in movies.

[00:08:28] He claims Drake has schemed for years, sending subliminal shots at numerous artists, including those who attacked him on Metro Boomin and Future’s latest two albums. Julius says Drake wanted the “20 v 1,” the underdog position and the comparison to Thanos. He praises Drake’s patience and delayed gratification, citing the lyric, “The lyrics begin to reveal themselves over time periods / Promise you’ll get that when the sky clears.” Julius says playing the long game brings rewards but requires patience few possess.

[00:09:17] Lesson five: never show your hand. Although the saying comes from poker, Julius applies it to chess: obvious opportunities let opponents build defenses, whereas the best moves catch them off guard. Linked to long-term thinking, this means waiting for the right opportunity to exploit a weakness; his sentence continues beyond the excerpt.

### G007 [00:09:40–00:11:14]

[00:09:40] Julius says an apparent opportunity may be an opponent’s trap. He recommends patience: position an offensive chess piece only when the time is right and it is too late for the opponent to defend or see the move coming.

[00:09:58] He says Drake’s mention of Kendrick’s fiancée Whitney hints at undisclosed knowledge without spelling it out. An explanation of “bodyguards like Whitney” connects it to *The Bodyguard*, starring Whitney Houston and Kevin Costner, in which a hired bodyguard and the woman he protects fall in love; Kendrick’s partner is also named Whitney, potentially implying she slept with her bodyguard. The speaker says Drake sometimes drags out words for emphasis, as on “Duppy Freestyle” concerning Pusha’s wife. He stresses the allegation is conditional: if Kendrick paid a man to protect Whitney and she was “[censored] around” with him, the line would be even more “[censored] crazy.” He says he was committed enough to watch the whole film with his girlfriend the previous night.

### G008 [00:11:16–00:12:56]

[00:11:16] The film did not do much for the speaker, but reminded him that Drake had mentioned it before. He argues that, given how calculated Drake is, its reappearance on a particularly scathing diss record is not incidental but a subliminal message Kendrick would understand even if listeners do not. An inserted Pusha T excerpt praises Drake as exceptionally good at subtle, under-the-radar lines. The speaker asserts that Kendrick has had plenty of issues with his wife and that Drake knows something: “where there’s smoke there’s fire.”

[00:12:14] He interprets Drake’s mention of a girl named Tokyo as another subliminal, aimed at Future and hinting at information Drake has not yet revealed. He speculates it might directly explain tension between the two. He identifies an Instagram user called “just Tokio,” shows her posts from Drake’s *It’s All a Blur* tour in Miami 28 weeks earlier—footage of Drake performing and a picture beside a trailer—and cautiously speculates Drake invited her for a particular reason.

### G009 [00:12:58–00:14:36]

[00:12:58] Continuing the Tokyo theory, the speaker says that a few months after the Drake show she posted birthday videos thanking her “Freebandz fam” for another celebration; he identifies Freebandz as Future’s label. Later she appeared front and center at Future’s Rolling Loud show, beside another trailer, and backstage wearing a *We Don’t Trust You* T-shirt, captioned “enough said” with the album’s release date. He says she had been linked to Future for years and shows a 2021 photo.

[00:13:40] He interprets Drake’s “I’m out in Tokyo, I’m big in Japan” as a sexual boast about the woman, whom he identifies as Japanese; a voice says, “I’m the only Japanese in the family.” He argues the line otherwise makes little sense because Japan is statistically one of Drake’s weakest markets.

[00:14:05] He says Drake later hints more directly that if Future’s “BM,” or baby mama, starts to “kiss and tell,” Future’s relationship with Travis could change. He notes that one of Future’s children’s mothers, Ciara, had a track called “Kiss & Tell,” and says his research found Future has eight children with eight different women. He begins narrowing the reference using the initials “BM.”

### G010 [00:14:40–00:16:10]

[00:14:40] The speaker identifies the woman as Britney Mey and says she and Future had a rocky relationship, including a recent child-support court battle that Future won. Julius compares Drake’s withholding of details to keeping chess pieces safe: Drake apparently has more to say, although he might instead be bluffing, itself a possible strategic move. He says Drake explicitly claims at the song’s end that he has not revealed everything he knows. Julius recommends conserving weapons and energy rather than expending everything in the first battle or round, and saving opportunities for the right time.

[00:15:25] Lesson six is “create dependencies.” Julius explains that strategically placed chess pieces can force an opponent to keep one piece stationary to protect another, weakening both offensively; an opponent might also depend on one of *your* pieces remaining in place, becoming vulnerable when it moves. He calls Drake and Metro Boomin especially strategic at creating dependencies: artists need Metro’s beats and know he can influence other artists, themselves dependent on him, not to work with them—almost like a political sanction.

### G011 [00:16:12–00:17:36]

[00:16:12] Julius says Drake likewise boasts of getting artists number-one hits: a Drake feature can make an album successful and launch a career, as he claims happened for some artists in the feud. He compares this to Henry Kissinger allegedly retaining political power by embedding himself so widely in political structures that removing him would cause chaos. Julius recommends making others at work depend on you and fear the consequences of losing you, creating leverage for compensation and promotion.

[00:16:47] Lesson seven concerns spectators rather than chess players. Julius says a bettor seeking the safest prediction would wait until near the end, but someone wanting the eventual winner’s credit for believing in them must choose earlier and accept more risk. As a chess game or war progresses, the likely winner becomes clearer; in war both sides also weaken, making the effect of additional aid easier to gauge. He recommends not committing early, but waiting until both sides weaken and then aiding the side likely to win.

### G012 [00:17:38–00:19:12]

[00:17:38] Julius suspects 21 Savage may be waiting for the right moment to choose a side. He says 21 has repeatedly stressed the importance of picking sides and is therefore unlikely to stay out entirely, but is in a difficult position: he was close to Metro Boomin during his rise, while a recent collaborative album with Drake significantly helped his career. Julius qualifies this as speculation and reiterates that the lesson holds whether or not 21 eventually chooses.

[00:18:18] He extends the recommendation to investing: before financially backing one of two competitors, let their conflict play out. He closes with what he calls the biggest lesson, law five from *The 48 Laws of Power*: “So much depends on reputation—guard it with your life.” Music follows.

# My First Fight - 5 Life Lessons

- Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=d-ozlIxnJK8
- Published (UTC): 2024-07-14T16:18:48+00:00
- Source: consolidated from timestamped transcript; NOT independently fact-checked

### G001 [00:00:00–00:01:53]

[00:00:00] Julius says he has been absent but not slacking: he worked harder over the past three months than ever before and wants to share what he learned about himself and life through a unique experience.

[00:00:31] Having things taken away made him appreciate freedoms he had taken for granted. Weight cutting prevented him from drinking or eating whatever he wanted, while a strict training schedule restricted his plans and bedtime. He missed an ice-cold beer, not counting calories, and even being able to eat an extra banana when hungry. Now that the process is over, he finds his renewed appreciation eye-opening.

### G002 [00:01:55–00:03:47]

[00:01:55] Julius reiterates that many things beyond those listed had been taken for granted throughout his life until they were stripped away. The process was extremely difficult, but the fight itself was the easy, fun part. He says he will show some fight clips, but not the whole fight, because he might fight again and does not want to provide too much free research.

[00:02:33] He enjoyed the fight and found it less exhausting than expected, which he attributes to the conditioning from an “insane,” brutal training camp. He describes pushing beyond what he thought his body could do, sometimes feeling close to passing out or vomiting; he believes those moments made him strong enough to perform well.

[00:03:21] Julius says physical or financial improvement requires putting oneself in uncomfortable situations. Without his crew and coaches pushing him past his perceived limits, he would have trained only to the point of slight discomfort, not nearly as hard.

### G003 [00:03:49–00:05:39]

[00:03:49] Julius says training alone would not have produced the skill and conditioning required for the fight. He generalizes that comfort or slight discomfort is unlikely to produce excellence: people may perform average to slightly above average depending on talent, IQ and genetic advantages, but, he says, true excellence requires extreme discomfort unless someone is an anomaly with an exceptional innate advantage.

[00:04:36] He had assumed he could endure any training and somehow did, but at points doubted whether he could handle it. Training extremely hard for a few days is different from doing so for three months, as injuries and fatigue compound, making each subsequent day exponentially harder.

[00:05:14] Despite some bad injuries, he returned to training the next day because missing it would compromise his potential performance and his crew might pull him from the fight, fearing he would make the gym look bad. He says he never contemplated quitting the project.

### G004 [00:05:42–00:07:21]

[00:05:42] Julius reiterates how injuries and fatigue compounded: rather than resting after an injury, he might worsen it the next day, pick up another, endure an especially rigorous session and still have a 5K to run later. He says this wore on his mind and body.

[00:06:15] Added to that was the constant pressure of having to perform before a huge crowd on a fixed date, while enduring the training and waiting for that day. The stress never went away for three months, but he thinks it is okay for him and relatable to others who excel under stress. His biggest achievements, he says, tend to occur in a state of constant stress or “constant war,” rather than comfort.

[00:07:06] He says compounding difficulties teach you about your toughness and willingness to persevere through anything.

### G005 [00:07:23–00:09:14]

[00:07:23] Julius feels that few life experiences match this challenge’s mental and physical difficulty. Completing a major challenge makes other things seem easier or trivial by juxtaposition.

[00:08:03] As an example of compounding injuries, he says a hard sparring shot that gives you a bloody nose may cause only mild pain and let you continue that day. The problem comes afterward: swelling and healing make even a light tap reopen the wound and cause heavy bleeding. His nose bled constantly for roughly the first three weeks of camp because it could not heal.

[00:08:57] Other injuries accumulated alongside it, including leg kicks he failed to check. He says adrenaline made those kicks barely noticeable during sparring, but he began feeling them on the walk home.

### G006 [00:09:17–00:10:45]

[00:09:17] Julius describes leg tightness appearing when stepping into the shower, getting up to use the bathroom at night and walking to training the next day. He says solid leg kicks produce a distinctive feeling beyond ordinary soreness that other fighters may recognize.

[00:09:41] He also mentions liver and kidney shots: a solid kick there hurts considerably more immediately than a bloody nose or leg kicks and leaves significant soreness for days.

[00:10:07] These injuries compounded with constant fatigue, soreness and, during his weight cut, persistent hunger and dissatisfaction. He ate lots of vegetables to make his stomach feel full, found rice cakes helpful and drank soda at night to feel full despite insufficient calories. All of this, he says, combined with constant pressure—not only about fight performance but other concerns he begins to introduce as the excerpt ends.

### G007 [00:10:47–00:12:35]

[00:10:47] Julius describes compounding pre-fight worries: making weight, medical or blood-work problems affecting him or his opponent, and the possibility that training would feel wasted. He says the pressure must simply be dealt with.

[00:11:14] Pushing through to the finish made him feel capable of overcoming almost anything. Though it sounds corny, he sincerely considers a first fight’s combination of physical and mental difficulty hard to match. It taught him about himself and increased his confidence beyond fighting. He twice clarifies that he is not advising everyone to fight, but suggests finding similarly uncomfortable, productive challenges.

### G008 [00:12:36–00:14:25]

[00:12:36] Julius says sustained, productive physical or mental discomfort can make people appreciate ordinary life more and become significantly better, even completely different, physically and mentally. He was confident before but is now much more so.

[00:13:17] He says confidence cannot be faked but must be earned: sparring several times weekly with experienced fighters and having his own fight made him confident in his fighting abilities and difficult to frighten, even if a large person confronts him at a bar or party. His remaining concern in a confrontation would be legal consequences—what cameras are watching and whether he could prove self-defense—not whether he could defend himself.

### G009 [00:14:27–00:16:12]

[00:14:27] Julius says challenging oneself toward a specific goal naturally produces doubts, including “what the [censored] am I doing?” He asked himself that once or twice in the first two weeks of fight preparation.

[00:14:56] Experienced sparring partners usually went easy on him as a novice, but trained much harder against him during fight camp for his own benefit. The contrast with the fun, technical sparring of regular training was challenging and discouraging; injuries compounded his doubts and impostor syndrome. He says similar questioning is normal in physical or mental challenges, such as starting a business and seeing no progress.

### G010 [00:16:14–00:17:57]

[00:16:14] Julius extends the business example to someone who has quit a job or invested heavily in a project and asks “what the [censored] am I doing?” He calls this low point normal and inevitable, though unhealthy, and part of a pattern.

[00:16:43] To escape that mindset early, he used “mind hypnosis” and studied the Law of Attraction. # “If I were not Alexander, then I should wish to be Diogenes" - Living True to Your Biology

- Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=EqKb-W0fNfE
- Published (UTC): 2026-05-14T17:40:08+00:00
- Source: consolidated from timestamped transcript; NOT independently fact-checked

### G001 [00:00:01–00:02:07]

[00:00:01] Julius deeply identifies with Alexander the Great’s purported statement, “If I were not Alexander, then I should wish to be Diogenes.” He describes a constant dilemma: he is naturally ambitious and, as evidence rather than an attempt at boasting, says that by 25 he had made millions, achieved financial freedom, run a business, and acquired supercars and a New York City penthouse. Yet he remains uncomfortable and hungry to conquer and ascend. Increasingly less materialistic, he says his ambition is less about money than the act of conquering and is beyond his control.

[00:01:17] Julius has diligently studied Stoicism for perhaps five years and believes he has made substantial progress, though he says none of us can be sages and he is nowhere near a Stoic sage; all are “progressors.” One area where he feels he has made no progress is being content without needing to conquer. He introduces a saying, unsure whether it came from Seneca, Marcus Aurelius, or Epictetus.

### G002 [00:02:11–00:03:56]

[00:02:11] The saying Julius recalls is approximately, “I have conquered the need to conquer.” He plans to post in a few days a currently unlisted video recorded weeks earlier about his admiration for his father, whom he considers genetically blessed in many ways. Although Julius says he has accomplished more financially on paper, he believes his father has accomplished more and lives a greater life: his father never felt Julius’s need to conquer and thus conquered it without trying, whereas Julius must try.

[00:03:04] Julius wonders whether he should try to conquer that need or instead embrace being Alexander. His philosophy is that living true to one’s biology produces the best quality of life. Though he finds much Stoicism congruent with that philosophy, he sees a dilemma in his inability to progress on this issue. He says he has conquered materialism, notwithstanding his nice car and penthouse, and asks listeners to take his word that he has become less materialistic.

### G003 [00:03:57–00:05:54]

[00:03:57] Julius reiterates that he has not conquered the need to conquer: he wakes with it and thinks almost constantly about conquering and ascending. For him, conquering can mean influence, bodily health, or other self-improvement, not just finance.

[00:04:32] He connects this to what he calls neurodivergent behavior: finding joy only in activities with a return on investment (ROI). As discussed in one of his first videos after returning to the channel, he is actively trying to enjoy non-ROI activities, but finds himself assigning returns even to those. For example, he tells himself girls find men who live freely attractive, like a man who goes surfing without worrying about making money during the day. A snort is heard.

[00:05:28] Calling that a tangent, Julius returns to whether trying to conquer his ambition is a mistake. He nevertheless considers the alternative ideal and agrees with the wisdom he sees in Stoicism and Diogenes; he interprets Alexander’s statement as agreement with that wisdom, which is why it resonates so strongly with him.

### G004 [00:05:57–00:08:04]

[00:05:57] Repeating Alexander’s purported quote, Julius interprets it as recognizing the wisdom of a person with no power or money and only enough food, water, and shelter to survive. He recounts Diogenes asking someone offering to do something for him merely to move out of his sunlight. Julius calls needing nothing true freedom and happiness: someone who has conquered the need to conquer has gained greater enjoyment and quality of life without material things.

[00:06:52] Though he considers that ideal, Julius believes living that way would conflict with his biology. He attributes his inherent ambition and desire to conquer to genetics, especially testosterone, beyond his control. Fighting his biological programming to replicate Diogenes’s life would, he believes, lower his quality of life. He similarly thinks his father is biologically programmed to be happy with an ordinary life. Julius speculates that his own ambition came through his mother’s side or a combination, although his paternal grandfather was also overwhelmingly ambitious, seemingly skipping a generation.

### G005 [00:08:06–00:10:03]

[00:08:06] Julius finds the possible generational skip in ambition peculiar. Whatever its genetic origin, he says environmental factors also contributed, all outside his control. Reiterating his position, he calls himself a determinist, as he says most physicists are, and dismisses compatibilism about free will as “cope.” One of his tattoos, “Fate,” expresses determinism in what he calls a pretty way.

[00:08:52] Since he did not choose how he is, Julius believes he is better off accepting and embracing it rather than fighting it. He recognizes Stoic wisdom and says he lives true to nearly all of it, but trying his hardest to live like Diogenes would create an internal imbalance and make him wake daily feeling something was wrong. He extends this to other areas of life, advocating living true to one’s biology and embracing one’s genetics and identity even when they contrast with societal norms or what society has programmed one to believe.

### G006 [00:10:06–00:12:03]

[00:10:06] Julius says living true to one’s biology yields the highest quality of experienced consciousness—what actually matters—even if life appears materially worse or lower-quality on paper. He acknowledges that this may run counter to wisdom such as Stoicism.

[00:10:38] He says he will link the video that inspired this discussion, by a creator he thinks is called Agora, whose philosophy summaries cover figures including Alexander and Julius Caesar. Julius recommends the channel and says its video explores Alexander’s statement in greater depth. He admires Alexander more than anyone who has ever lived and identifies with him on many levels.

[00:11:25] Repeating the Alexander–Diogenes quote, Julius finds Alexander’s introspection and wisdom remarkable. He says people who do not read the history and nuances of Alexander’s interactions, as Julius has, see him merely as a violent conqueror and miss his true brilliance.

### G007 [00:12:04–00:12:23]

[00:12:04] Julius emphasizes the subject’s young age, then discusses his mysterious death at 31: some conspiracy theories suggest poisoning, but Julius considers sickness or disease more likely. [00:12:19] He says he often has visions that he will die in the same way, around age 30 or 31.

[00:00:05] Julius says Robert Plomin was asked a question his own viewers often ask: what genetics means for free will. # just let go

- Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=m9zmK_Ioob4
- Published (UTC): 2026-05-20T17:29:15+00:00
- Source: consolidated from timestamped transcript; NOT independently fact-checked

### G001 [00:00:00–00:02:08]

[00:00:00] Julius says he is out in “normieville,” can see his home, and is taking a walk for steps and perhaps a “performative cigarette.” He likes seeing regular people enjoying life rather than being lost in thought.

[00:00:39] He says people must eventually stop caring what others think and accept that some things cannot be changed, despite looksmaxers encouraging continued coping; he claims most of what actually matters is unchangeable. He contrasts living in delusion that hinders quality of life with accepting reality. Losing weight or getting a tan can help, especially at the far end of the spectrum, and he does not discourage such basics, but says they eventually reach diminishing returns and one must accept one’s position in life.

### G002 [00:02:11–00:04:15]

[00:02:11] Julius says his recurring advice to live congruently with one’s biology and embrace oneself circles back to the “turbo normie” advice to be yourself. He says learning about “neurodivergent autistic” matters was not a complete waste: being oneself and living congruently with genetics and biology requires understanding these “dark truths.” They are dark only if perceived that way; nature simply is, neither good nor bad, like a spider eating a fly.

[00:03:19] He says accepting what lies outside one’s control is difficult, and describes the community as split and nearly in civil war. He says superficial people call genetic determinists like himself “tumors,” which he rejects; he calls the other side delusional looksmaxers doing censored things. He claims many are autistic and risk facial harmony by treating surgery as more than a means of correcting facial flaws.

### G003 [00:04:18–00:06:16]

[00:04:18] Continuing, Julius says trying to reach “Chad level” through surgery is a losing gamble: perhaps a one-in-a-million outlier could achieve natural harmony, but the overwhelming majority cannot. He says people expend energy believing such efforts will change things, while wasting time, harming their mental health and disrupting their lives; they would be better off adopting stoicism and accepting the unchangeable.

[00:05:12] He reiterates that accepting genetics does not make his side “doomers”: in his view, acceptance requires strength, while those who keep coping and refuse reality are weak.

[00:05:58] He says letting go brings peace while still doing “objectively good” things, such as reaching a low, healthy body-fat level—not out of insecurity, but because he considers it objectively good.

### G004 [00:06:17–00:08:16]

[00:06:17] Julius adds going to the gym and building a nice physique as objectively good, but says other efforts have diminishing returns. He reiterates that peace comes from accepting and making the best of one’s hand in life, although that is easier said than done and some receive better hands than others.

[00:06:49] He recounts seeing a little person in a wheelchair on his way there. He nearly recorded him as an example for viewers, not to mock him, but could not bring himself to do it partly because the man might somehow see the video. [00:07:39] He condemns what he calls gaslighting people about their difficulties, exemplified by telling them they are not ugly, are ugly on the inside, or are responsible for their problems. He introduces suicide as an interesting, somewhat spontaneous phenomenon, leaving the thought unfinished.

# Video Programming to help you stop being a b!tch

- Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=zxTCGMl_KBg
- Published (UTC): 2026-05-24T16:10:14+00:00
- Source: consolidated from timestamped transcript; NOT independently fact-checked

### G001 [00:00:00–00:01:59]

[00:00:00] Julius says earlier discussions about living true to one’s biology for a better quality of life focused mostly on dating, reproduction, and embracing one’s alpha or beta nature according to genetics. He now wants to address society’s programming people against traits they possess because of evolutionary success.

[00:00:52] He says his philosophy is not red-pill tough-guy advice, though it overlaps with red-pill or alpha behavior: it is about living true to one’s biology in every aspect despite societal suppression. He claims evolutionary success required a combination of hawkish and dovish tendencies, not an excess of either. Constantly fighting everyone is unsuccessful, he begins to explain, even for the dominant individual or biggest lion.

### G002 [00:02:05–00:03:51]

[00:02:05] Continuing the lion example, Julius claims a habitual fighter accumulates injuries despite winning many fights and may die before reproducing; even if he reproduces and his genes are diluted through his partner, offspring sharing those genetics may also fight too much to reproduce. Conversely, he says, the excessively dovish—modern-day cowards completely afraid to fight—were also weeded out.

[00:02:53] He argues that people watching today must have a reasonable combination of both tendencies somewhere within them. People occupy a spectrum of natural aggression, which he ties to behavioral genetic predispositions and hormones, especially testosterone, which he says is primarily genetic. Almost nobody watching is completely dovish, he claims, but society makes people behave that way as the supposedly correct way to operate, against their biology; he begins to qualify that this might be true to some people’s biology.

### G003 [00:03:58–00:05:53]

[00:03:58] Julius allows that exceptional people with zero testosterone who are “completely wired to be a bitch” might be best served by excessive dovishness, but says outliers do not make the rule. For the majority, he considers embracing their hawkish tendencies and balancing them important to quality of life, despite society’s efforts to suppress them.

[00:04:42] He recommends that a realistic man not fear fighting, even someone much bigger or stronger, when justified and when backing down would cause substantial emotional turmoil. Recalling prior videos, he says failing to respond to a “beta test” might avoid physical injury and immediate embarrassment but leave trauma for months or years, potentially worse than the fleeting embarrassment of losing. His main point is not to fear losing to someone with a biological advantage.

### G004 [00:06:00–00:07:38]

[00:06:00] Julius adds training advantages: he realistically expects he would lose to John Jones, but if being emasculated, would rather fight and lose. He argues observers would recognize Jones’s lifelong training and status as the world’s best fighter, so losing would be less embarrassing than imagined and might earn more respect for courage than embarrassment.

[00:06:53] He extends this to less extreme mismatches: people expect a much bigger person to win, so the bigger person has more to lose. Referring to the previous video, he stresses being perceived as justified—an innocent victim of bullying who stands up and defends himself.

### G005 [00:07:42–00:09:30]

[00:07:42] Julius says losing while defending oneself has less drastic consequences than imagined, whereas shying away can have greater consequences, lingering in one’s thoughts for months, years, or forever and shaping one’s reputation. He argues that willingness to fight, even in defeat, can be better for long-term physical safety and avoiding embarrassment.

[00:08:35] He reasons that even big, hawkish bullies have dovish tendencies and may avoid a smaller or less experienced person known to fight back and inflict some damage. In his illustrative scenario, a bully considering someone occasionally seen at a local bar recalls stories of him fighting a bigger man and continues the example in the next group.

### G006 [00:09:35–00:11:19]

[00:09:35] In Julius’s illustrative scenario, the smaller man lost but made the bigger man’s nose bleed, so the prospective bully chooses another target. ### G004 [00:06:23–00:08:32]

[00:08:02] Reading the AI’s response, he says it called “epistemic wall banging” the most precise term for the exhaustion and “Semmelweis reflex” or “paradigm inertia” the psychological phenomenon. He is unsure how to pronounce Semmelweis and asks listeners to bear with him.

### G005 [00:08:36–00:10:41]

### G006 [00:10:44–00:12:48]

[00:11:25] He repeats Google’s “epistemic wallbanging” and notes another listed concept, “epistemic inertia fatigue”: exhaustion from fighting a system or crowd using outdated circular logic, such as “this is true because we’ve always said it’s true.” He considers that close, but says “epistemic wallbanging” apparently is the term and does not roll off the tongue.

[00:12:02] Julius says their informal dictionary does not always need a word, just a quick way to convey a shared idea or feeling. ### G007 [00:12:50–00:14:49]

In his cave analogy, a person who left the cave saw reality and could contrast it with the shadows, but the still-shackled cave dwellers violently defend what they know when he tries to explain; they have not encountered the new idea, are closed-minded, and do not care.
- [00:14:03] When tired of people who resist new enlightenment and regurgitate consensus or an earlier hypothesis, Julius recommends saying, “Just get back in your cave.” He calls it a concise, casual, somewhat comedic and satirical way to close the discussion that need not be too serious and rolls off the tongue.

### G008 [00:14:51–00:16:39]

- [00:15:22] He finds it funny that Plato was also frustrated by this and that someone like himself, described with a censored word, independently and unprovoked began thinking about the same things. Laughter follows. He adds that he disagrees with much of what Plato says and does not necessarily love him, but attributes their disagreements not to Plato’s intelligence but to his lack of exposure to data available to them.
- [00:16:04] Julius clarifies that highlighting “midwit” behavior does not mean he considers himself above midwits; he describes himself with another censored word. # Life gets better when you stop trying to control narratives

- Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=_wi3-W29H9Q
- Published (UTC): 2026-06-24T16:28:28+00:00
- Source: consolidated from timestamped transcript; NOT independently fact-checked

### G001 [00:00:01–00:01:50]

[00:00:01] Julius says life gets much better when, with some nuance, one lets go of controlling narratives and being outcome-dependent—practices he calls stoic. He nearly succumbed to that temptation that morning and caught himself before replying; he offers the incident as an everyday illustration of how such impulses can go unnoticed, whether the stakes are significant or not.

[00:01:05] He describes a funny Instagram reel by a comedian spoofing “day in the life” videos: instead of an exciting activity, it invites viewers to watch reels at a friend’s house. Julius commented on it the previous night; his comment had about 6,000 likes in 19 hours.

### G002 [00:01:53–00:03:23]

[00:01:53] Julius woke up to replies that tempted him to control the narrative, though he stopped himself. His comment was: “I don't know about physically showing your phone. In reality you just DM them while in the same room.” In the reel, the comedian physically shows his friend the phone.

[00:02:14] Julius explains that the joke plays on people becoming more atomized and the somewhat dystopian but common habit of watching reels all day: physically showing someone the phone would be too much human engagement compared with DMing them *in the same room*. He imagines viewers protesting in partly censored language that he needn’t explain, but says many “retards” replying missed the joke. Others agreed or laughed because, whether or not they understood the joke, they saw some truth and humor in it.

### G003 [00:03:24–00:05:41]

[00:03:24] Julius says things are funny partly because they contain truth. As an example of a reply apparently missing his joke, he cites RetroTheKami: “why DM if bro in front of me,” calling it an unfortunate case of IQ. Looking for more examples, he wonders whether some replies were removed and checks his notifications.

[00:04:28] He finds a reply from a name he tentatively pronounces “Tain Gatocura”: “Just say you don't have real friends.” He initially mocks the reply and its four likes, amid laughter, then realizes “real” was spelled **REEL**. Using censored self-deprecation, he says he likely missed the other person’s joke, is glad he didn’t correct him, and admits he failed to catch it on first reading. He allows that it could have been a spelling mistake but thinks a joke is very likely.

### G004 [00:05:44–00:07:31]

[00:05:44] Julius reiterates that the “reel” reply was probably a joke, but maintains that some people, including the “why DM if bro is right in front of me” commenter, don’t get his joke; he was tempted to explain it to them.

[00:06:22] Laughing, he says the “reel” realization affected him because he had been banking on that reply as the most telling example for the video. He again uses censored self-deprecation and says acknowledging the mistake in real time is authentic, raw and organic—something he says viewers don’t see elsewhere on YouTube. He presents this as not controlling the narrative: he doesn’t care whether people think he is intelligent and says life is better when they can think what they want. Had he corrected the commenter without recognizing the possible pun, he says, he would have faced the stress of a reply pointing out that *he* missed the joke.

### G005 [00:07:33–00:09:35]

[00:07:33] Julius calls that hypothetical embarrassment a consequence of trying to control the narrative and recommends not “extending yourself,” referring viewers to his video explaining the phrase. He returns to his uncertainty about whether “reel” was a pun or a misspelling, asks viewers what they think, and leans toward a joke he missed. He says they will blur the commenter because his kids are shown and leaving that visible is “not cool.”

[00:08:47] He recommends letting disagreeable Instagram or YouTube comments stand rather than always trying to control the narrative. He says Clavicular used to be good at not caring or controlling narratives but has declined considerably, frequently engaging and replying to people on Twitter now; Julius thinks this is connected to his attempt to portray a good side.

### G006 [00:09:36–00:11:24]

[00:09:36] Julius says Clavicular is trying to shift from a bad-guy persona to a virtuous one, which he regards as a difficult and generally undesirable transition for an online persona, and says the subject deserves its own video. In Julius’s account, Clavicular gained his following by mocking people and saying censored things without consequence, not by trying to be good. As an example, Julius says that on Adin Ross’s private jet, when asked who was responsible for ruining the country, Clavicular answered “probably black people and Mexicans.” Julius argues that subsequently trying to assert “I’m a good person” is not a seamless change.

[00:10:36] Julius says that if Clavicular is actually a good person, it will naturally show without his needing to convince people through replies and statements. He recalls what he calls a performative Twitter statement about standing up for women’s rights in Paris, and another, less certainly remembered, about Baklava treating waitresses improperly and Clavicular standing up for his staff. Julius says this is out of character and an attempt to control the narrative; his sentence trails off.

### G007 [00:11:26–00:13:16]

- [00:11:26] Julius continues that the previously discussed behavior does not work out well. He says Stoicism preaches against it because incongruence can cost supporters and, internally, it is stressful.
- [00:11:48] He recommends letting go and not caring if people think he is [ __ ], ugly, rude, or an [ __ ]; he says he really does not care.
- [00:12:11] Julius says he is practicing not controlling the narrative but is not perfect and may slip up. He invites Discord members to point it out if they catch him doing it on Twitter, imagining he would acknowledge they were right, and offers to help them do the same.
- [00:12:39] Reiterating that narrative control is bad, he says to let events pan out: people who will think you are [ __ ] or evil will do so regardless of the control mechanism used. He claims successful narrative control usually requires highly strategic, indirect methods to convince above-average-intelligence people, while those at the left end of the IQ spectrum are usually easier to convince. He begins offering Sneako as an example.

### G008 [00:13:19–00:14:20]

- [00:13:19] Julius claims Sneako has a good following because he uses narrative-control tactics that work primarily on the left end of the IQ spectrum. He characterizes most of Sneako’s supporters as more susceptible to manipulation and performative acts.
- [00:13:49] Wrapping up, Julius reiterates not to control narratives. He says he could have replied to people by explaining that they missed his joke, but instead should let them think he is [ __ ] and was making a factual statement about sending reels by DM while in the same room. - Source: consolidated from timestamped transcript; NOT independently fact-checked

### G001 [00:00:00–00:02:15]

[00:00:00] Julius says Carlyle, whom he addresses with a censored term, understood hundreds of years ago that parliamentary government is theater: a spectacle of interest and eloquence.

[00:00:16] He digresses about World Cup excitement in Little Italy. Although he does not follow sports, he enjoys seeing people excited, as he did when the Knicks were winning and people celebrated while he was little in Little Italy. He rejects “midwits” who condemn ordinary people for enjoying sports, joking that he is not a midwit but has an 87 IQ; some language is censored.

[00:01:08] Returning to Carlyle, Julius says he predicted the future and described democracy as the illusion that voting can substitute for leadership. He contrasts it with Alexander the Great, Julius Caesar, Napoleon and other great men, whom he describes as rare individuals whose combination of traits allowed them to lead nations. He claims genetics helps explain their exceptional qualities and that the present system prevents similarly rare, genetically gifted people from rising to the top.

### G002 [00:02:17–00:04:14]

[00:02:17] Julius says the loudest, most unscrupulous and performative people rise instead. He credits Carlyle with identifying virtue signaling hundreds of years before it became an everyday concept.

[00:02:54] He calls “all politicians are liars” a superficial observation and explains that democracy requires lying, performance and corruption for success; moral people are unseen because they fail. Even honest small-town mayors may succeed but struggle, he says, because exposure requires money and lobbying. He moves from saying corruption is very likely to calling it guaranteed, and argues that democracy is not broken but functioning precisely as designed.

### G003 [00:04:17–00:06:22]

[00:04:17] Julius reiterates that voting is an illusion of leadership: it comforts the masses by making them feel powerful, while they actually lack power and are easily manipulated. Invoking the IQ bell curve, he says high-IQ people are a small minority, most are average, and skepticism and critical thinking require a degree of above-average IQ; consequently, the voters with majority power are easily manipulated.

[00:05:28] He gives this as one reason he avoids politics, but says his primary reason is Stoicism: one should not worry about what is beyond one’s control. Against the objection that a vote provides some control, he weighs its microscopic effect against the enormous energy and life invested in politics, calling it a bad trade-off that leaves one with almost no control.

### G004 [00:06:24–00:08:34]

[00:06:24] Julius concludes there is no reason to engage in politics. He praises Clavicular’s phrase “Politics are jester” and his making that attitude cool for young people. Julius recommends feeling above political back-and-forth and “sloppy” YouTube videos exposing contradictions by “midwits like AOC”: he says such content may appeal at 15 or 16, but people should graduate beyond it.

[00:07:20] He describes watching left and right fight from a bird’s-eye view. Although he acknowledges it sounds conspiratorial, he says this division and distraction of the masses is part of democracy’s design and benefits those in power. It also lets the wealthiest pursue their interests because successful politicians must be corruptible; thus the most unscrupulous, rather than the most competent, rise.

### G005 [00:08:36–00:10:40]

[00:08:36] Julius says voting left or right, loving or hating Trump, makes no difference: every successful politician in a democracy is a puppet to some degree, with no exceptions, though some hide it or perform better than others. [00:09:36] He asks what choice voters have, saying candidates will not be the most competent or most likely to improve ordinary people’s quality of life. Genuine change is possible when the most competent person rises, he argues; competence does not mean highest IQ alone, but a combination of genetic qualities producing an exceptional individual. A brief other voice says, “The shoes fit, then.” Julius begins arguing that hereditary nobility had some benefit.

### G006 [00:10:44–00:13:09]

[00:10:44] Julius argues that passing nobility down a family could, to a degree, be better than democracy because genetics are inherited. If both king and queen had good genetics, he says, a prince would probably, though not certainly, inherit a reasonably good recombination, potentially better if they acted eugenically.

[00:11:20] He calls eugenics a concept from the last hundred years, but claims people thousands of years ago recognized inheritable characteristics—including race, height, behavioral tendencies and intelligence—even without a term such as DNA. In his view, genetic inheritance helps explain why keeping rule in a family was not entirely unreasonable and why that system lasted so long.

[00:12:15] Julius says neither he nor Carlyle considers hereditary rule ideal; he attributes to Carlyle the view that it had run its course. Julius favors a system in which the most competent can rise, which he says democracy prevents. He reiterates that democracy is an illusion and not broken: although it does less for everyday quality of life than people think, it serves its intended purpose, which must be understood.

### G007 [00:13:13–00:15:14]

- [00:13:13] Julius says the previously discussed arrangement was not for the viewer, but to deceive them into feeling comfortable and in control.
- [00:13:20] He remarks that the “[ __ ] bikes” are back, jokes that they will be stoic and unbothered, and says someone has to turn one on and off because it has occasional issues. He has treated himself to a good, sugar-free cappuccino instead of his usual black coffee.
- [00:13:56] He says he has covered most of what he wanted and encourages interested viewers to read Carlyle, whom he considers far ahead of his time in predicting democracy’s course and in other respects.
- [00:14:30] Julius reiterates that he does not care about politics or intend to start voting; he likes observing human nature and history and understanding how things work. He hopes his observations help viewers detach from politics if his explanation that political energy yields no ROI and they have no control was insufficient. His next phrase about votes is unclear; he begins calling it a system before the group ends.

### G008 [00:15:17–00:18:00]

- [00:15:17] Julius calls the system an illusion and a game, asking whether participation makes viewers feel stupid. He mockingly imagines admiring Trump for calling out a Hillary Clinton lie during a debate.
- [00:15:52] He calls politics a spectacle, a theater of eloquence and interest, where the most accomplished virtue-signaling performers succeed. He says deception, performance and lying are rewarded, as is being strategically “the most scrupulous” without being completely caught and deemed immoral. He claims the system works well for powerful people and lobbyists.
- [00:16:52] Again asking whether engagement makes one feel like a sucker, he imagines those in power looking at people as “[ __ ] retards” for debating and watching Ben Shapiro while thinking themselves smart for spotting contradictions. He asks whether they have not grown past that since age 16.
- [00:17:29] He compares this endless loop to a video he recorded earlier that day: incels repeatedly watch videos condemning hypergamy and promiscuous women. He says the audience already knows this and should graduate past it, stop engaging in the conversation and stay above it: “You’re better.”

### G009 [00:18:02–00:18:47]

[00:00:17] In a casual exchange, someone asks for change for a $20 bill; another person thinks they have a five. A Skittle and two gums are mentioned, and the speaker says to keep the change and “adios amigo.” He then says, “As you can see, I’m [ __ ] [ __ ], but you know, we rock with it.”

[00:00:58] The censored word reminds Julius of the “Boomer Truth Regime.” He predicts it will become an identifier or code word: people soon will struggle to distinguish “AI people” from authentic people, then clarifies that he means people trapped inside the simulation who cannot break free of the regime because they fear uttering a single word. In his account, saying the censored word will identify someone who has broken free—a truly free human with critical-thinking ability who is unafraid of “fake consequences.”

[00:02:06] Asked whether that is in their future, Leo says he feels the world will become a little worse. Julius agrees that is probably where they are headed.

### G002 [00:02:25–00:04:27]

[00:02:25] Julius says he does not like trying to control narratives and is fine if people call him racist and hateful. He recommends letting go, focusing on what one can control and stopping caring, attributing that outlook to Stoics such as Seneca and Marcus Aurelius.

[00:02:48] He says “gracias,” remarks that someone is not used to him ordering milk, and says he is treating himself. He is trying to enjoy ordinary things because he can really enjoy only ROI activities. After a brief music interlude, he says he is consciously trying non-ROI activities, such as smoking a cigarette in Little Italy and enjoying the vibe.

[00:03:38] He might watch the World Cup to blend in with neurotypical people; although he would have to fabricate some emotions and pretend to be interested, he thinks blending in is a good exercise for neurodivergent people.

[00:04:04] Asked what he wants to be remembered for, Julius answers “genetics”: passing down his genes by having many children. He repeatedly calls having children and leaving a legacy the most important thing and what “we’re here for,” then begins, “As Richard Dawkins once said,” before the excerpt ends.

# why you experience joy and pain - embracing your design

- Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=qXpniY_SjVw
- Published (UTC): 2026-07-05T18:21:27+00:00
- Source: consolidated from timestamped transcript; NOT independently fact-checked

### G001 [00:00:00–00:02:05]

[00:00:00] Julius says Robert Plomin described having and raising children as “unparalleled emotional enjoyment.” A clip says, “I’d have as many kids as I could,” and that love for one’s children is deep because evolution designed it that way. Julius agrees there is nothing else like the experience.

[00:00:28] Julius recounts Plomin’s comparison to the Marines: after a couple of drinks, parents, like people who served, may say it was great but they probably would not do it again. Julius says the unparalleled enjoyment and fulfillment are present but not necessarily registered while going through it; afterward, one does not necessarily say one would do it again just because one remembers every emotional spike.

[00:01:36] Julius attributes much of this to Plomin’s explanation that offspring are, on average, 50% genetically similar to a parent. He mentions parents and siblings as other close relatives, and identical twins as 100% similar. A navigation voice interjects, “Keep left.”

### G002 [00:02:08–00:04:00]

[00:02:08] Julius says parents also learn to appreciate the 50% differences as a child grows into who they are. In a clip, Plomin says genetics pushes people to have children and makes the relationship rewarding because a child is 50% genetically like the parent. He contrasts this with a claimed genetic correlation of about .1 with a spouse: people select someone somewhat like themselves, especially in intelligence, which he calls the most highly assortative aspect of mating. He says parents can marvel at a child genetically becoming who they are, rather than trying to make the child what they want.

[00:03:15] Julius recommends letting children make themselves rather than making them into something: they do not have 100% of the parent’s genetics, and he says environmental influence will not hold up. Referring to his previous discussion of “heritability snowballing,” he claims people increasingly become who they truly are as they age because they create their environments. He calls environment widely misunderstood and mentions his hour-long discussion video on it, but does not delve into it here.

### G003 [00:04:02–00:05:58]

[00:04:02] Julius reiterates that trying to shift a child into what a parent desires will not work or be sustainable and creates incongruence. He says to appreciate the differences, including resemblance to the spouse, and marvel—as Plomin put it—at the child becoming their own person. For Julius, the unique combination of similarities and differences makes watching a child grow uniquely rewarding.

[00:05:00] Julius says there is more to the subject than Plomin addresses, though Plomin says evolution designed reproduction to be rewarding. In a clip, Plomin says humans are designed to have children and he would have as many as he could. He says choosing not to have children is fine and he does not want to cause anxiety, but too few people call having children the most wonderful thing in life. He contrasts the deep love for children with romantic love, which he says changes, and describes parenting as going with rather than fighting one’s evolutionary flow.

### G004 [00:06:00–00:07:59]

[00:06:00] The clip continues that parenting is not always easy but is very rewarding. Julius cautions that evolution is pragmatic and had no conscious design, so “designed” should not be taken too literally. He claims reproduction is rewarding because, if it were not, humans would not be here.

[00:06:32] Julius says the connection goes deeper than childbirth and watching a child grow: everyday behavior relates to reproduction even when people are not consciously thinking about children. He claims most people do not plan having children and that in many countries most now marry afterward. He says everything people find rewarding or punishing directly relates to their likelihood of and progress toward having children, although 99.99% are unaware of it.

[00:07:38] Julius recalls Discord users arguing when he first raised this that people can “hack” or trick the brain, as with drugs, and its evolutionary tendency to reward progress toward reproduction.

### G005 [00:08:01–00:09:45]

[00:08:01] Julius illustrates what he sees as reproductive rewards: food supports survival and health, making one more attractive and likely to find a partner; caring for one’s health and going to the gym feel rewarding for the same reason. Closer to a relationship, a reply from someone whose number one obtained gives dopamine hits and, if one really likes them, butterflies.

[00:08:43] He says someone with no dating experience talking to one girl may feel such intense butterflies that logic goes out the window: mind and emotions focus on the path to reproduction. He attributes clouded judgment and being tricked in “beta bucks” or gold-digger scenarios to biological hardwiring and emotional flooding, especially when the person is one’s only option or by far one’s best genetic option—for example, a girl much better-looking than the others, whom one marvels at and feels an intense connection with. Texting her repeatedly produces those feelings.

# No ones "crazy"...

- Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=x4ovirYSM24
- Published (UTC): 2026-07-09T19:02:50+00:00
- Source: consolidated from timestamped transcript; NOT independently fact-checked

### G001 [00:00:00–00:01:54]

[00:00:00] Julius says he recently realized he has never called or simply judged someone crazy. A thought experiment prompted this: although he believes his casual genetic analysis of people is truthful, he imagines that talking that way in ordinary life would make others call him weird or crazy. Trying to see their perspective, he recalled that he usually understands why someone thinks as they do.

[00:01:19] He may judge their conclusion wrong, though he hesitates over “incorrect,” citing Nietzsche for the idea that the only thing we know is that we know nothing. Often he understands an idea he considers wrong because he once held it himself and has since “graduated” beyond that thought process or philosophy.

### G002 [00:01:56–00:03:47]

[00:01:56] Continuing his metaphor, Julius says he has been in that “cave” and become further enlightened, so he understands where the person is in their journey rather than calling them crazy. He claims some people remain stuck at a phase depending on their IQ or general intelligence.

[00:02:37] For example, when someone states a wild conspiracy theory, he may recognize a narrative he has also seen on Twitter and understand why it appears plausible and is strongly believed; he does not dismiss the person as crazy. More interesting to him are ideas so bizarre and novel that he cannot trace how someone reached them. In those cases, he says, he shuts up and listens rather than dismissing them.

### G003 [00:03:49–00:05:41]

[00:03:49] Julius says listening does not mean assuming the person is right or necessarily more enlightened—often they are not—but he wants to understand their thought process. If someone said “2 + 2 is 5,” he would initially suspect they were joking or pretending to be crazy. If they were utterly convinced and offered unfamiliar nuances and rationale, he would want to know how they came to believe something so far from the shared understanding of logic.

[00:04:57] One possible explanation, he says, is that the person has taken substances that alter their mind and distort their relation to reality; a dissociative, for example, might leave them somewhat separated from reality and using atypical logic, but does not make them crazy. Another possibility is that they read something or went down an online rabbit hole.

### G004 [00:05:45–00:07:38]

[00:05:45] Julius describes a rabbit hole with convincing, accumulating material as a kind of hypnosis: reviewing it can reveal why it persuaded someone, even if the same trick would not work on oneself. He calls “2 + 2 is 5” an extreme case that might require some degree of hypnosis.

[00:06:36] He contrasts that with everyday propaganda, which he characterizes as a more realistic, less advanced form of manipulation. In his account, a conspiracy theory is easier to sell because it could be grounded in reality, whereas “2 + 2 = 5” is not and would require advanced methods. Even then, he says, one can reverse-engineer the material and understand the person as a victim of their own mind combined with exposure, rather than as crazy. He introduces heritability as another possible part of the discussion.

### G005 [00:07:40–00:09:26]

[00:07:40] Julius says the process is not only environmental: behavioral tendencies also help lead people into rabbit holes, and some are particularly fascinated by conspiracy theories. He reiterates that propaganda is frequent in everyday life.

[00:08:06] He recalls eating breakfast with his cousin at a Florida hotel, where a woman he calls a sweetheart saved food for them after the 10 a.m. closing time. After they had talked with her and she became comfortable, she pointed out plane trails through the window—“See what they’re doing?”—and expressed strong belief in chemtrail conspiracies.

[00:08:52] He says he did not consider her crazy. He compares understanding her thinking to why he will never fear darkness or anything: break it down, and darkness is simply the absence of light photons. In his account, her mind was more susceptible to being convinced by material.

### G006 [00:09:28–00:11:18]

[00:09:28] Julius says someone created the conspiracy and supplied enough evidence and logical reasoning to convince a large demographic. He claims that for many susceptible people belief becomes beyond their control once they encounter such material; even apart from a discussion of determinism and no free will, he says, genetic susceptibility means it is not their fault.

[00:10:11] He reiterates that such people are not crazy, while qualifying that it depends on the definition: one could define “crazy” as easily believing propaganda designed to influence thought. As he understands its common usage, however, the word is dismissive. When he hears a bizarre idea held with conviction, he instead tries to reverse-engineer how the person reached it; possible reasons include drugs, which he reiterates do not themselves make someone crazy.

### G007 [00:11:20–00:13:17]

[00:11:20] Julius says the response previously discussed is rational: it makes sense that the person’s body reacts that way and their brain is not operating as it should.

[00:11:39] He realizes he does not think he has ever called someone “crazy.” He briefly interrupts himself, saying he thinks someone may have called the police and that a worker is talking to them, though he is unsure.

[00:12:11] Saying he was wrapping up anyway, he reiterates his main point: rather than dismiss someone as crazy, he reverse-engineers their thought process and understands why they think that way. Often he once thought similarly but has since “graduated” beyond it—for example, he remembers having certain ideas at age 16.

[00:12:55] He reintroduces “graduate,” a word he often uses for becoming further enlightened out of a particular cave, invoking the allegory of the cave: one was once in that cave but has graduated beyond it to new ideas.

# Stop blindly trusting studies! #science

- Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=cWhbzFZDWYE
- Published (UTC): 2026-07-16T21:01:19+00:00
- Source: consolidated from timestamped transcript; NOT independently fact-checked

### G001 [00:00:00–00:01:38]

- [00:00:00] Julius says studies blatantly lie and make people who regurgitate them thinking they sound smart look like fools. He says the example is from Stuart Ritchie’s *Science Fictions*, adding, “you’re not listening to a [censored] here.” It concerns publication bias and P-hacking, which he says has two flavors.
- [00:00:34] He describes the subtler flavor, “re-hypothesizing.” He says publication requires a P value below .05 for statistical significance, which he describes as meaning the result did not happen by chance or accident. He says that threshold is hard to achieve, especially in psychology, which he characterizes as full of false, random theories and pseudoscience.
- [00:01:06] He says researchers whose results do not support their original theory adjust their analysis—for example, looking only at men’s or only at women’s data—until they obtain P < .05 and can publish. He reiterates the publication point, then introduces a supposedly even crazier practice.

### G002 [00:01:39–00:02:57]

- [00:01:39] Julius calls the other practice “harking”: conducting studies without a hypothesis and devising one after seeing the results. Sarcastically asking whether that is “awesome,” he compares it to a Texas sharpshooter firing randomly at a barn, painting bull’s-eyes afterward, and claiming to have hit them everywhere.
- [00:02:19] He calls this publication bias and urges people to stop blindly trusting studies or YouTubers who cite them to seem smart, saying the studies are often a result of publication bias.
- [00:02:36] Referring to a gap in published studies, he says the expected pattern has smaller studies at the bottom, with greater variation in effect sizes—some very big and some very small. He says the very small ones are missing in reality because they go into the “file drawer”; his final sentence, “They don’t get…,” is cut off. A snort is heard during this discussion.

# How antidepressants passed FDA approval (loophole explained)

- Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=u7lsEOFUwQA
- Published (UTC): 2026-07-21T22:12:32+00:00
- Source: consolidated from timestamped transcript; NOT independently fact-checked

### G001 [00:00:00–00:01:55]

[00:00:00] Julius recalls results of 38 positive and 36 negative trials, expressing disbelief that they barely made the cut through a “loophole” after 74 trials; he jokes they could at least have aimed for 40 positive results and wonders why this is not widely known. Music plays intermittently.

[00:00:38] He asks how the FDA approved medications with what he calls weak efficacy data and significant side effects: sexual dysfunction, long-term weight gain, insomnia, nausea and diarrhea. He says antidepressants have been linked to increased suicidal ideation in children and young adults, increased stroke and all-cause mortality risks in older adults, and miscarriage in pregnant women; he claims surviving offspring are very likely to be like him, with autism and “birth malf” [unfinished].

[00:01:22] He says the topic comes not just from a censored self-description but from Dr. Stuart Ritchie’s *Science Fictions*, discussed in his previous video, about how fraud, bias, negligence and hype undermine the search for truth. He attributes approval to an FDA criteria loophole, speculates it might be intentional, but says he will take off his “tinfoil hat” for this video.

### G002 [00:01:57–00:03:36]

[00:01:57] Julius says speculation is unnecessary because there is concrete evidence viewers have been lied to and exploited for profit. He dislikes how Hollywood-dramatic that sounds, since such YouTube claims are usually untrue, but insists this one is true. He predicts the video will reveal a “sea of deception” and make viewers more skeptical of studies, which people often accept unquestioningly as authorities; he promises to explain how to question them later.

[00:02:44] Unlike his previous video on blatant scientific fraud, this one concerns subtler publication bias, which he says takes various forms and helped antidepressants and many other highly profitable drugs gain FDA approval. Before discussing tactics he says trick the public and FDA, he introduces the “serotonin myth”: the familiar, appealing explanation that depression means too little serotonin and antidepressants raise it, solving the problem. He says there was never really evidence for this and attributes the term to psychologist Irving Kirsch. Music continues intermittently.

### G003 [00:03:38–00:05:22]

[00:03:38] Julius says Kirsch’s “myth” does not deny serotonin exists or that antidepressants affect it; rather, scientists never found convincing evidence that depressed people consistently have lower serotonin than others. He says studies of a different antidepressant that lowered rather than raised serotonin produced extremely similar findings, calls this a neglected wake-up call, and tentatively says the drug was approved in France “or something.” He promises to explain the similar effects later.

[00:04:23] He describes research measuring serotonin in blood and metabolites, examining receptors, and experimentally lowering serotonin in healthy volunteers to see whether depression resulted. He says findings were inconsistent—some studies found differences, many did not—and a large systematic review found no clear pattern that low serotonin simply causes depression.

[00:04:53] He says the chemical-imbalance theory became popular because it was easy to explain, fitted the drugs’ brain-chemistry effects and was extensively marketed by pharmaceutical companies. He compares its logic to concluding headaches are caused by insufficient aspirin because aspirin helps them, which he calls nonsense. Music is intermittent.

### G004 [00:05:25–00:07:14]

[00:05:25] Julius states Kirsch’s point that a treatment changing a biological system does not prove illness arose from a deficiency in that system: increased serotonin does not prove depression was caused by low serotonin, just as alcohol affects GABA but alcoholism is not caused by lack of alcohol.

[00:05:46] He says a 2022 umbrella review led by Joanna Moncrieff examined decades of evidence and found no consistent support for depression being caused by reduced serotonin activity or concentration. He qualifies that serotonin could still play a role in mood and the brain is much more complicated, but says the simple chemical-imbalance explanation and the idea that antidepressants correct it lack evidential support.

[00:06:21] He asks how companies convinced the FDA and, through a trickle-down effect, doctors, psychologists, therapists and other apparent adult authorities that a pill could solve or improve depression beyond placebo. He stresses that depression is real and causes suffering, although he suggests viewers might end up thinking it is not real and that this could be an advantageous, placebo-like mindset. He reiterates that depression is real and says genetics predispose some people more than others. Music is intermittent.

### G005 [00:07:16–00:08:50]

[00:07:16] Julius says there is no single depression gene; tens of thousands of genes influence it. He calls the influence of generalist genes on one psychiatric trait “polygenicity” and explains “pleiotropy” as one gene influencing many traits, making this possible despite there being only a few tens of thousands of genes. He says genetics is much more complex than the one-gene-one-effect understanding of 10–15 years ago, and reiterates that depression and differing predispositions are real.

[00:08:01] A voice, apparently from an inserted discussion, says predisposition to depression arises through predispositions to other things, but predispositions do not mean nothing can be done. The speaker says depression is poorly defined and compares it with intelligence: there is no intelligence object measurable with a ruler in the brain; rather, intelligence is inferred as a latent variable from positive correlations among different tests and explains roughly half their variation. Music continues intermittently.

### G006 [00:08:52–00:10:21]

[00:08:52] The discussion speaker asks whether depression can similarly be inferred as a single underlying thing from symptoms such as insomnia, low mood and sometimes crying for no reason. The speaker cites a long-known researcher, whose name is transcribed uncertainly as “Frerieded,” as arguing that there need not be one underlying entity; instead, attention should go to a network of symptoms that interact and cause one another—for example, insomnia causes low mood, which causes anger at a spouse. Statistical approaches can explore that network, unlike a model in which depression itself causes all symptoms.

[00:09:53] Julius says the evidence suggests that although depression is real, a pill has no more efficacy than placebo; he immediately qualifies that it has a little more and promises to explain what that difference means and how it arose. He suggests that, if someone could convince their mind depression is not real, deliberately manipulating that belief might have effects very similar to taking a placebo.
