### G007 [00:10:22–00:11:46]

[00:10:22] An incomplete remark refers to something that might be possible at the end of the video. Julius asks how companies and professionals convinced the world if the evidence suggests otherwise. He claims SSRIs and even serotonin-reducing antidepressants, such as one approved in France, have much smaller benefits than most believe—about the same as a placebo—because of publication bias and selective reporting. Music is heard.

[00:10:49] Julius introduces an interview in which Stuart Ritchie discusses what Julius calls a horrifying 2008 study of studies. Ritchie says almost all negative studies were never submitted for publication, while almost all positive ones were. Of the few negative studies published, some shifted from a depression measure on which no result was found to another that produced a result, dredging the data; others spun null trials as promising. He begins comparing the resulting literature to a laundering process.

### G008 [00:11:48–00:13:30]

[00:11:48] Ritchie continues that the “laundered” literature bears little relation to the studies actually conducted. He finds this scary, thinks it happens across fields, and says the same paper found it in therapy as well as antidepressant trials. Nevertheless, he thinks that after adjusting for such issues, including replication bias, antidepressants appear to have a small effect on depression; even if serotonin is not the mechanism, randomized controlled trials suggest they do something, and he does not think the mechanism matters in that case. Music is heard.

[00:12:31] Julius identifies the paper as *Selective Publication of Antidepressant Trials and Its Influence on Apparent Efficacy*, published in the *New England Journal of Medicine*, and calls it one of the greatest demonstrations of publication bias. He says researchers obtained every antidepressant trial submitted to the FDA, including unpublished ones: of 74 trials, the FDA judged 38 positive and 36 negative or questionable. Almost every positive study appeared in journals, most negative studies disappeared, and some negative studies were written to look positive.

### G009 [00:13:32–00:15:24]

[00:13:32] Julius says the published literature made 94% of studies look positive, whereas the FDA judged only 51% positive. He says he had ChatGPT make a visual contrasting the close real proportions with the published picture. He questions whether therapists, psychologists and people’s parents can be blamed for saying the drugs work when the truth was hidden so sneakily through publication bias.

[00:14:15] Julius claims selective publication led the literature to overestimate antidepressant effectiveness by roughly 32% overall—not necessarily because researchers lied, but because negative studies went unpublished, were spun or had endpoints changed. He says Stuart Ritchie discusses these mechanisms in *Science Fictions* and promises to explain them so viewers can recognize lies; he claims the replication crisis extends far beyond antidepressants and is involved in everything.

[00:15:08] In a hypothetical, a tiny real effect produces 10 studies finding nothing and 10 getting lucky; only the latter are published, so a meta-analysis reports 10 positive papers and the audience draws a positive conclusion.

### G010 [00:15:27–00:17:21]

[00:15:27] Julius finishes the hypothetical: there were actually 20 experiments, but half disappeared. He calls this the “file drawer problem” and says he will later discuss HARK/HARKing, p-hacking, outcome switching and multiple comparisons, all explained in *Science Fictions*. He presents these as tactics that distort truth and reasons not to believe every study.

[00:16:06] Julius says Irving Kirsch similarly used Freedom of Information requests to obtain FDA trial data, and including unpublished trials made the antidepressant–placebo difference much smaller than most believed. He stresses that Kirsch does not say antidepressants never work: the claimed average benefit above placebo is small, but still needs explanation. Julius says Kirsch suspects “breaking blind” and cites one study in which 89% of patients receiving the drug correctly guessed they had the real antidepressant, a result he says is extremely unlikely by chance. ### G011 [00:17:23–00:18:58]

[00:17:23] Julius says patients can identify the real drug, even if its efficacy is in question, because its noticeable side effects—including nausea and diarrhea—are not in question; an expletive before “side effects” is censored. He argues that recognizing the drug breaks the blinding meant to make the study fair and increases the placebo effect because patients believe it could work. By contrast, believing one has a placebo would, he says, negate its potential effect.

[00:18:42] Julius says this shows why people must think critically: studies do not spell out this reality, and professors, mainstream media and doctors will not teach or tell it. Music accompanies parts of the discussion.

### G012 [00:18:59–00:20:39]

[00:18:59] Julius reiterates that people must think for themselves and claims such problems occur across all fields of science. He offers to explain other tactics used to lie to people so they can be more aware.

[00:19:20] In a file-drawer hypothetical, a researcher gives 100 patients either a new antidepressant or placebo; after six months the drug does not outperform placebo. ### G013 [00:20:41–00:22:17]

### G014 [00:22:18–00:24:06]

- [00:24:46] He attributes approval despite weak efficacy data to an FDA “loophole”: he says two adequately conducted trials need only show a statistically significant drug–placebo difference, with no limit on how many trials can be run to find those two; negative trials do not count, and clinical significance is not considered.

# Dark truth I realized when dating 2 girls at once for 2 years (Gianna & Bella P1)

### G001 [00:00:00–00:02:04]

[00:00:00] Julius begins the story of Giana and Bella, previously alluded to in his videos, including an account of their falling out in a video about a girl from a Caribbean island. He says the experience taught him niche, nuanced lessons about female nature: he was not exactly either woman’s boyfriend, but had the benefits of exclusivity and girlfriend-like behavior without exchanging titles.

[00:01:04] After a brief “Ciao, gracia … It’s okay. Thank you,” he says delaying the title is deliberate and impactful. The names are pseudonyms, with context available in a Discord guide. His first girlfriend, Bree, was the only woman to whom he had given the title, after a year; she was fantastic, and he broke up with her not because she did anything wrong, but because he would not have a family with her. He leaves the fuller story for another day. Music is audible intermittently.

### G002 [00:02:06–00:04:10]

[00:02:06] Julius reiterates that he had a great time with Bree and no complaints about her character, and says she was his only actual girlfriend. His first lesson is to prolong the process because women must earn both the girlfriend title and exclusivity, or at least the idea of it. He says he was not exclusive, although at one point he agreed to be and blatantly lied.

[00:02:45] He was comfortable lying because he rationalized it. Referring to a prior response to Aesthetics Waiting, he says anything can be rationalized: that person might rationalize avoiding fights, while Julius might rationalize the benefits of being willing to engage in an altercation. He has convinced himself that lying is in both his and the women’s interests—their net happiness, quality of life and future—though he acknowledges this could merely be rationalization and he could be completely wrong. He attributes his belief to what he calls the laws of female nature: women get more joy and entertainment from relationships with drama and suspicion.

### G003 [00:04:12–00:06:03]

[00:04:12] Julius says, while acknowledging more nuance, that suspicion makes women feel loved, feel intensely, dream about a man, become obsessed and have purpose. He attributes this to hypergamy: a man who is obviously genetically far out of a woman’s league would produce similar feelings, and such behavior implies the same idea. He claims non-exclusivity consequently makes relationships more interesting and fun for women.

[00:05:12] He says he was exclusive and never cheated when he had a girlfriend, and thinks he probably would be again if he gave someone the title, then qualifies that he does not know. Not wanting to appear to claim he is a good person, he says to assume he will continue lying. Julius says the idea was discovered in 2017, but AI and ChatGPT-type technology did not take off until around 2021, when people began investing heavily and finding it scalable with GPUs. [00:15:50] James distinguishes Navier-Stokes’ practical applications from the particular theoretical result, which he says has none and cannot generate even one dollar for OpenAI. He asks why OpenAI spends resources on such problems and reiterates his earlier hypothesis: it wants people to believe solving theoretical math implies it can cure cancer or deliver other “snake oil” promises. He says an Altman interview does exactly that.

### G010 [00:16:48–00:18:36]

[00:16:48] The James clip continues with his paraphrase of Altman’s interview: solving theoretical math supposedly shows AI is close to curing cancer or other diseases and generating substantial revenue. James calls the inference “total BS.”

[00:17:07] Julius says the next layer is more than understanding AI as a “probabilistic parrot” and large language models as neither magical nor sentient: it is recognizing that the public is being fooled, deceived and manipulated. He says his own video also shows this and places it in his comparison, briefly asking how to remove something.

### G011 [00:18:37–00:20:36]

[00:18:37] Julius calls the investment point highly nuanced and says Luke, an unidentified woman and another man are incapable of understanding it.

[00:18:56] Julius presents the incomplete revelation hypothesis as an argument against the efficient market hypothesis. He summarizes the latter as public information being priced into the market immediately, making financial news and articles pointless to read; he says he agrees, but introduces a qualification.

[00:19:37] He says important public information can be buried in lengthy, boring, repetitive documents full of legal terminology—for example, a revealing finding about how bad Anthropic’s and OpenAI’s debt situation is. He asks why “smart money” would not find such information and go beyond avoiding AI investment to shorting it.

### G012 [00:20:38–00:22:37]

[00:20:38] Julius’s answer is that smart money knows most people will not read the documents, so it does not make the bet and the information never gets priced into the market. If only a few smart people see information that would reveal an investment to be bad, he says it can remain a good investment to a degree.

[00:21:22] Julius uses Leopold’s face as an example while qualifying that Leopold specifically was probably lucky rather than especially sharp. He says some hedge-fund managers understand Altman is a “scammer” and “snake oil salesman”; they may not understand the technology themselves, but have computer scientists explaining the S-curve, dominating constraints and lack of magic in LLMs. Nevertheless, they invest because they think they can make more money before the bubble bursts: this is smart money gambling.

[00:22:31] Julius calls Patrick Boyle a smart investor who does not short AI; his explanation continues beyond the excerpt.

### G013 [00:22:38–00:24:26]

- [00:22:38] Julius says the previously discussed person does not short AI but avoids investing in hype stocks. A smart gambler, by contrast, might expect an AI bubble to pop yet invest, recognizing that “the market could stay irrational longer than you can stay solvent.” He says many hedge fund managers make this gamble, while reiterating his view that Leopold got lucky with the paper that blew up.
- [00:23:24] Julius says there are hundreds of thousands or millions of realization layers, branching into nuanced subsets. ### G014 [00:24:28–00:26:08]

- [00:24:28] Julius calls AI one of the more complex examples, saying realization layers also appear in jokes and other contexts. His favorite example is the “normie” advice “just be yourself”: in his AI-chart analogy, the old man at the bottom says it, but one can arrive at it again at the top.
- [00:25:07] He describes that route as going through red pill, black pill and looksmaxing, then realizing looksmaxing has diminishing returns. In his view, the final stage is accepting genetics’ weight and that many looksmaxes and, in many cases, red-pill tactics do not substantially change outcomes for many people—bringing them full circle to “just be yourself.”

### G015 [00:26:10–00:27:48]

- [00:26:10] Julius compares viewers who have come full circle to his earlier example of Leopold at the far right, aware of the layers yet investing in AI. He clarifies that Leopold is only a *pretend* smart hedge-fund investor in the analogy: he does not want to credit him.

### G016 [00:27:50–00:29:00]

- [00:27:50] Julius continues that normies do not follow their own advice because they do not know how to be themselves or who they are at a genetic level. Nonetheless, he says everyone eventually becomes and is themselves, invoking “heritability snowballing,” which he says he has discussed often.
